↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JOSEPH remover or increaser. (1.) The elder of the two sons of Jacob by Rachel (Genesis 30:23, 24), who, on the occasion of his birth, said, “God hath taken away [Hebrews ‘asaph] my reproach.” “The Lord shall add [Hebrews yoseph] to me another son” (Genesis 30:24). He was a child of probably six years of age when his father returned from Haran to Canaan and took up his residence in the old patriarchal town of Hebron. “Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age,” and he “made him a long garment with sleeves” (Genesis 37:3, R.V. marg.), i.e., a garment long and full, such as was worn by the children of nobles. This seems to be the correct rendering of the words. The phrase, however, may also be rendered, “a coat of many pieces”, i.e., a patchwork of many small pieces of divers colours. When he was about seventeen years old Joseph incurred the jealous hatred of his brothers (Genesis 37:4). They “hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.” Their anger was increased when he told them his dreams (37:11). Jacob desiring to hear tidings of his sons, who had gone to Shechem with their flocks, some 60 miles from Hebron, sent Joseph as his messenger to make inquiry regarding them. Joseph found that they had left Shechem for Dothan, whither he followed them. As soon as they saw him coming they began to plot against him, and would have killed him had not Reuben interposed. They ultimately sold him to a company of Ishmaelite merchants for twenty pieces (shekels) of silver (about $2, 10s.), ten pieces less than the current value of a slave, for “they cared little what they had for him, if so be they were rid of him.” These merchants were going down with a varied assortment of merchandise to the Egyptian market, and thither they conveyed him, and ultimately sold him as a slave to Potiphar, an “officer of Pharaoh’s, and captain of the guard” (Genesis 37:36). “The Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake,” and Potiphar made him overseer over his house. At length a false charge having been brought against him by Potiphar’s wife, he was at once cast into the state prison (39; 40), where he remained for at least two years. After a while the “chief of the cupbearers” and the “chief of the bakers” of Pharaoh’s household were cast into the same prison (40:2). Each of these new prisoners dreamed a dream in the same night, which Joseph interpreted, the event occurring as he had said. This led to Joseph’s being remembered subsequently by the chief butler when Pharaoh also dreamed. At his suggestion Joseph was brought from prison to interpret the king’s dreams. Pharaoh was well pleased with Joseph’s wisdom in interpreting his dreams, and with his counsel with reference to the events then predicted; and he set him over all the land of Egypt (Genesis 41:46), and gave him the name of Zaphnath-paaneah. He was married to Asenath, the daughter of the priest of On, and thus became a member of the priestly class. Joseph was now about thirty years of age. As Joseph had interpreted, seven years of plenty came, during which he stored up great abundance of corn in granaries built for the purpose. These years were followed by seven years of famine “over all the face of the earth,” when “all countries came into Egypt to Joseph to buy corn” (Genesis 41:56, 57; 47:13, 14). Thus “Joseph gathered up all the money that was in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, for the corn which they bought.” Afterwards all the cattle and all the land, and at last the Egyptians themselves, became the property of Pharaoh. During this period of famine Joseph’s brethren also came down to Egypt to buy corn. The history of his dealings with them, and of the manner in which he at length made himself known to them, is one of the most interesting narratives that can be read (Genesis 42-45). Joseph directed his brethren to return and bring Jacob and his family to the land of Egypt, saying, “I will give you the good of the land of Egypt, and ye shall eat the fat of the land. Regard not your stuff; for the good of all the land is yours.” Accordingly Jacob and his family, to the number of threescore and ten souls, together with “all that they had,” went down to Egypt. They were settled in the land of Goshen, where Joseph met his father, and “fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good while” (Genesis 46:29). The excavations of Dr. Naville have shown the land of Goshen to be the Wady Tumilat, between Ismailia and Zagazig. In Goshen (Egyptian Qosem) they had pasture for their flocks, were near the Asiatic frontier of Egypt, and were out of the way of the Egyptian people. An inscription speaks of it as a district given up to the wandering shepherds of Asia. Jacob at length died, and in fulfilment of a promise which he had exacted, Joseph went up to Canaan to bury his father in “the field of Ephron the Hittite” (Genesis 47:29-31; 50:1-14). This was the last recorded act of Joseph, who again returned to Egypt. “The ‘Story of the Two Brothers,’ an Egyptian romance written for the son of the Pharaoh of the Oppression, contains an episode very similar to the Biblical account of Joseph’s treatment by Potiphar’s wife. Potiphar and Potipherah are the Egyptian Pa-tu-pa-Ra, ‘the gift of the sun-God.’ The name given to Joseph, Zaphnath-paaneah, is probably the Egyptian Zaf-nti-pa-ankh, ‘nourisher of the living one,’ i.e., of the Pharaoh. There are many instances in the inscriptions of foreigners in Egypt receiving Egyptian names, and rising to the highest offices of state.” By his wife Asenath, Joseph had two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:50). Joseph having obtained a promise from his brethren that when the time should come that God would “bring them unto the land which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob,” they would carry up his bones out of Egypt, at length died, at the age of one hundred and ten years; and “they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin” (Genesis 50:26). This promise was faithfully observed. Their descendants, long after, when the Exodus came, carried the body about with them during their forty years’ wanderings, and at length buried it in Shechem, in the parcel of ground which Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor (Joshua 24:32; comp. Genesis 33:19). With the death of Joseph the patriarchal age of the history of Israel came to a close. The Pharaoh of Joseph’s elevation was probably Apepi, or Apopis, the last of the Hyksos kings. Some, however, think that Joseph came to Egypt in the reign of Thothmes III. (see PHARAOH), long after the expulsion of the Hyksos. The name Joseph denotes the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh in Deuteronomy 33:13-17; the kingdom of Israel in Ezekiel 37:16, 19, Amos 5:6; and the whole covenant people of Israel in Psalm 81:4. (2.) One of the sons of Asaph, head of the first division of sacred musicians (1 Chronicles 25:2, 9). (3.) The son of Judah, and father of Semei (Luke 3:26). Other two of the same name in the ancestry of Christ are also mentioned (3:24, 30). (4.) The foster-father of our Lord (Matthew 1:16; Luke 3:23). He lived at Nazareth in Galilee (Luke 2:4). He is called a “just man.” He was by trade a carpenter (Matthew 13:55). He is last mentioned in connection with the journey to Jerusalem, when Jesus was twelve years old. It is probable that he died before Jesus entered on his public ministry. This is concluded from the fact that Mary only was present at the marriage feast in Cana of Galilee. His name does not appear in connection with the scenes of the crucifixion along with that of Mary (q.v.), John 19:25. (5.) A native of Arimathea, probably the Ramah of the Old Testament (1 Samuel 1:19), a man of wealth, and a member of the Sanhedrim (Matthew 27:57; Luke 23:50), an “honourable counsellor, who waited for the kingdom of God.” As soon as he heard the tidings of Christ’s death, he “went in boldly” (lit. “having summoned courage, he went”) “unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus.” Pilate having ascertained from the centurion that the death had really taken place, granted Joseph’s request, who immediately, having purchased fine linen (Mark 15:46), proceeded to Golgotha to take the body down from the cross. There, assisted by Nicodemus, he took down the body and wrapped it in the fine linen, sprinkling it with the myrrh and aloes which Nicodemus had brought (John 19:39), and then conveyed the body to the new tomb hewn by Joseph himself out of a rock in his garden hard by. There they laid it, in the presence of Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of Joses, and other women, and rolled a great stone to the entrance, and departed (Luke 23:53, 55). This was done in haste, “for the Sabbath was drawing on” (comp. Isaiah 53:9). (6.) Surnamed Barsabas (Acts 1:23); also called Justus. He was one of those who “companied with the apostles all the time that the Lord Jesus went out and in among them” (Acts 1:21), and was one of the candidates for the place of Judas.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s peeled rods. Jacob’s scheme to acquire the speckled and striped sheep involves peeling stripes into branches and placing them in the watering-troughs while the flocks breed, on the assumption that visual exposure during conception affects offspring patterning. The technique reflects pre-genetic ANE agricultural folk-belief — the same belief underwrites a number of ancient breeding practices. Modern readers tend to ask whether the technique "really worked"; the narrator’s answer is theologically located: the breeding succeeds because Yahweh prospers Jacob (cf. 31:9, "God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me"; 31:11–12, the angelic dream confirming divine-orchestrated breeding outcomes). The chapter is doing two things at once: portraying Jacob’s ANE-typical pre-scientific practice and asserting that the success comes from divine intervention rather than from the practice itself. The verse offers one of the OT’s most striking cases of folk-technology framed within providence-theology.

↩ ◇ Note. The teraphim theft. Rachel’s theft of her father’s household idols is one of the OT’s most discussed single details. The teraphim (small household figurines, probably ancestral) likely had legal-inheritance significance in Mesopotamian household practice — the bearer of the teraphim could claim primary inheritance rights, attested in Nuzi tablets. Rachel’s theft therefore may have functioned as a final claim on Laban’s household property (cf. 31:14, where Rachel and Leah complain that Laban has treated them as foreigners and withheld their inheritance). The theft’s narrative consequence is significant: when Laban catches up and searches the camp, Rachel hides the teraphim under a camel-saddle and refuses to rise "because the way of women is on me" (31:34–35) — using menstruation-impurity to keep her father from approaching the saddle. The episode is one of Genesis’s most layered: female agency, household-religion, inheritance-claim, and ritual-impurity all combine in a single brief sequence. Most strikingly, it shows household-idol religion within the patriarchal-line family — a messy reality the narrator records without comment.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GILEAD hill of testimony, (Genesis 31:21), a mountainous region east of Jordan. From its mountainous character it is called “the mount of Gilead” (Genesis 31:25). It is called also “the land of Gilead” (Numbers 32:1), and sometimes simply “Gilead” (Psalm 60:7; Genesis 37:25). It comprised the possessions of the tribes of Gad and Reuben and the south part of Manasseh (Deuteronomy 3:13; Numbers 32:40). It was bounded on the north by Bashan, and on the south by Moab and Ammon (Genesis 31:21; Deuteronomy 3:12-17). “Half Gilead” was possessed by Sihon, and the other half, separated from it by the river Jabbok, by Og, king of Bashan. The deep ravine of the river Hieromax (the modern Sheriat el-Mandhur) separated Bashan from Gilead, which was about 60 miles in length and 20 in breadth, extending from near the south end of the Lake of Gennesaret to the north end of the Dead Sea. Abarim, Pisgah, Nebo, and Peor are its mountains mentioned in Scripture.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DEW “There is no dew properly so called in Palestine, for there is no moisture in the hot summer air to be chilled into dew-drops by the coldness of the night. From May till October rain is unknown, the sun shining with unclouded brightness day after day. The heat becomes intense, the ground hard, and vegetation would perish but for the moist west winds that come each night from the sea. The bright skies cause the heat of the day to radiate very quickly into space, so that the nights are as cold as the day is the reverse, a peculiarity of climate from which poor Jacob suffered thousands of years ago (Genesis 31:40). To this coldness of the night air the indispensable watering of all plant-life is due. The winds, loaded with moisture, are robbed of it as they pass over the land, the cold air condensing it into drops of water, which fall in a gracious rain of mist on every thirsty blade. In the morning the fog thus created rests like a sea over the plains, and far up the sides of the hills, which raise their heads above it like so many islands. At sunrise, however, the scene speedily changes. By the kindling light the mist is transformed into vast snow-white clouds, which presently break into separate masses and rise up the mountain-sides, to disappear in the blue above, dissipated by the increasing heat. These are ‘the morning clouds and the early dew that go away’ of which Hosea (6:4; 13:3) speaks so touchingly” (Geikie’s The Holy Land, etc., i., p. 72). Dew is a source of great fertility (Genesis 27:28; Deuteronomy 33:13; Zechariah 8:12), and its withdrawal is regarded as a curse from God (2 Samuel 1:21; 1 Kings 17:1). It is the symbol of a multitude (2 Samuel 17:12; Psalm 110:3); and from its refreshing influence it is an emblem of brotherly love and harmony (Psalm 133:3), and of rich spiritual blessings (Hos. 14:5).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DROUGHT From the middle of May to about the middle of August the land of Palestine is dry. It is then the “drought of summer” (Genesis 31:40; Psalm 32:4), and the land suffers (Deuteronomy 28:23: Psalm 102:4), vegetation being preserved only by the dews (Hag. 1:11). (See DEW.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GALEED heap of witness, the name of the pile of stones erected by Jacob and Laban to mark the league of friendship into which they entered with each other (Genesis 31:47, 48). This was the name given to the “heap” by Jacob. It is Hebrew, while the name Jegar-sahadutha, given to it by Laban, is Aramaic (Chaldee or Syriac). Probably Nahor’s family originally spoke Aramaic, and Abraham and his descendants learned Hebrew, a kindred dialect, in the land of Canaan.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JEGAR-SAHADUTHA pile of testimony, the Aramaic or Syriac name which Laban gave to the pile of stones erected as a memorial of the covenant between him and Jacob (Genesis 31:47), who, however, called it in Hebrew by an equivalent name, Galeed (q.v.).

↩ ◇ Note. The Mizpah benediction. Laban’s closing blessing at Mizpah ("the Lord watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another") has had perhaps the longest devotional afterlife of any single Genesis verse, used as a parting blessing in countless Christian liturgies and as the textual root of the modern "Mizpah" jewelry tradition (broken-heart pendants exchanged at separations). The verse’s narrative context complicates its devotional use significantly: Laban’s "blessing" is in fact a wary boundary-treaty, more covenant of mutual deterrence ("if you afflict my daughters, or take other wives… God is witness," 31:50) than warm valedictory wish. The two parties have just spent twenty years deceiving each other; the Mizpah pillar marks the territorial line they will not cross. The verse’s history of devotional use is one of the OT’s clearest examples of a phrase outliving its narrative context entirely — its weight in modern Christian piety has nothing to do with what it actually means in Genesis 31. The chapter is also significant for naming the place "Galeed" (Hebrew "heap of witness") and "Mizpah" ("watchtower"), two of Genesis’s many name-etiologies.

↩ ◇ Note. Esau’s embrace. The reunion is one of Genesis’s most emotionally complex scenes: Jacob has spent the previous chapter terrified of Esau’s vengeance, dividing his camp for safety, sending elaborate gifts, wrestling with God all night for the strength to face his brother — and Esau simply runs, embraces, kisses, and weeps. The expected violence does not materialize. The brother who was supposed to kill Jacob (cf. 27:41) instead enacts forgiveness so complete that Jacob says "I have seen your face as one sees the face of God, and you have accepted me" (33:10). The line connects the encounter with Esau directly to Jacob’s previous-night encounter with God at Peniel (32:30, "I have seen God face to face"). The parallel is theological: Jacob meets God in his struggling brother just as he met God at the ford. Esau, in his moment of unexpected mercy, becomes the divine face. The episode is one of the OT’s most extraordinary portraits of forgiveness — not earned, not negotiated, simply offered. Walter Brueggemann reads ch 33 as one of the canon’s most surprising theological moments.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: INSTANCES OF, FORGIVENESS, JACOB, KISS, LEAH.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept'. Ephrem reads the reconciliation of the brothers as a foretaste of the eschatological reconciliation promised in Rom 11:25-26 (the fullness of the Gentiles, then all Israel saved). Tewahedo ecumenical theology — preserved in the long Tewahedo refusal to demonize other communions even during Chalcedonian controversies — draws on the Esau-Jacob embrace as canonical model for inter-Christian relations.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SHALEM perfect, a place (probably the village of Salim) some 2 miles east of Jacob’s well. There is an abundant supply of water, which may have been the reason for Jacob’s settling at this place (Genesis 33:18-20). The Revised Version translates this word, and reads, “Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem,” thus not regarding it as a proper name at all.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: HAMOR, LAND, SHECHEM.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HAMOR he-ass, a Hivite from whom Jacob purchased the plot of ground in which Joseph was afterwards buried (Genesis 33:19). He is called “Emmor” in Acts 7:16. His son Shechem founded the city of that name which Simeon and Levi destroyed because of his crime in the matter of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter (Genesis 34:20). Hamor and Shechem were also slain (ver. 26).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KESITAH (Genesis 33:19, R.V., marg., a Hebrew word, rendered, A.V., pl. “pieces of money,” marg., “lambs;” Joshua 24:32, “pieces of silver;” Job 42:11, “piece of money”). The kesitah was probably a piece of money of a particular weight, cast in the form of a lamb. The monuments of Egypt show that such weights were used. (See PIECES.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SHECHEM shoulder. (1.) The son of Hamor the Hivite (Genesis 33:19; 34). (2.) A descendant of Manasseh (Numbers 26:31; Joshua 17:2). (3.) A city in Samaria (Genesis 33:18), called also Sichem (12:6), Sychem (Acts 7:16). It stood in the narrow sheltered valley between Ebal on the north and Gerizim on the south, these mountains at their base being only some 500 yards apart. Here Abraham pitched his tent and built his first altar in the Promised Land, and received the first divine promise (Genesis 12:6, 7). Here also Jacob “bought a parcel of a field at the hands of the children of Hamor” after his return from Mesopotamia, and settled with his household, which he purged from idolatry by burying the teraphim of his followers under an oak tree, which was afterwards called “the oak of the sorcerer” (Genesis 33:19; 35:4; Judges 9:37). (See MEONENIM.) Here too, after a while, he dug a well, which bears his name to this day (John 4:5, 39-42). To Shechem Joshua gathered all Israel “before God,” and delivered to them his second parting address (Joshua 24:1-15). He “made a covenant with the people that day” at the very place where, on first entering the land, they had responded to the law from Ebal and Gerizim (Joshua 24:25), the terms of which were recorded “in the book of the law of God”, i.e., in the roll of the law of Moses; and in memory of this solemn transaction a great stone was set up “under an oak” (comp. Genesis 28:18; 31:44-48; Exodus 24:4; Joshua 4:3, 8, 9), possibly the old “oak of Moreh,” as a silent witness of the transaction to all coming time. Shechem became one of the cities of refuge, the central city of refuge for Western Palestine (Joshua 20:7), and here the bones of Joseph were buried (24:32). Rehoboam was appointed king in Shechem (1 Kings 12:1, 19), but Jeroboam afterwards took up his residence here. This city is mentioned in connection with our Lord’s conversation with the woman of Samaria (John 4:5); and thus, remaining as it does to the present day, it is one of the oldest cities of the world. It is the modern Nablus, a contraction for Neapolis, the name given to it by Vespasian. It lies about a mile and a half up the valley on its southern slope, and on the north of Gerizim, which rises about 1,100 feet above it, and is about 34 miles north of Jerusalem. It contains about 10,000 inhabitants, of whom about 160 are Samaritans and 100 Jews, the rest being Christians and Mohammedans. The site of Shechem is said to be of unrivalled beauty. Stanley says it is “the most beautiful, perhaps the only very beautiful, spot in Central Palestine.” Gaza, near Shechem, only mentioned 1 Chronicles 7:28, has entirely disappeared. It was destroyed at the time of the Conquest, and its place was taken by Shechem. (See SYCHAR.)

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. El Elohe Yisrael (אֵל אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל) — "God, the God of Israel." Jacob’s altar at Shechem bears one of Genesis’s most theologically dense names: El (the broader Northwest Semitic divine name, used as title or proper name across Canaanite religion) is named as Elohei Yisra’el ("the God of Israel"). The naming registers Jacob’s identity-shift after Peniel — he is now Israel, and his altar identifies the deity as his God, the God specifically of his line. The construction "El the God of Israel" also works theologically as identification: the high god El of the broader Levantine pantheon is named here as functionally identical with the deity who has shepherded Jacob. Most modern OT scholarship (so Cross, Smith) reads such constructions as evidence of the gradual Israelite absorption of El-traditions into Yahwism — Yahweh and El were not always identified, but the patriarchal narratives increasingly identify them as the same. Jacob’s altar-name preserves an older theological moment, before that identification was fully developed. The verse is one of the OT’s most important pieces of evidence for the historical development of Israelite monotheism.

↩ ◇ Note. The rape of Dinah. The chapter opens with one of the OT’s starkest portrayals of sexual violence: Shechem, the prince of the local city, takes Dinah and "humbles her" (Hebrew vay’anneha, the same verb used of sexual violation throughout OT law — Deut 22:24, 29). The narrative complications begin immediately: Shechem then "loved the young woman" (34:3) and proposes marriage. The text refuses easy readings — what begins as violation transitions into proposed alliance, and Dinah herself never speaks. Phyllis Trible’s and Mieke Bal’s feminist readings have made this chapter central to OT scholarship on gendered violence and silence. The brothers’ vengeance — Simeon and Levi’s deceitful slaughter of all the Shechemite men, while convalescent from circumcision — Jacob deplores but does not retract; his deathbed curse on Simeon and Levi (49:5–7) traces directly to this episode. The chapter encodes one of the OT’s most morally unresolved single narratives.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s realpolitik. Jacob’s rebuke of Simeon and Levi after their slaughter at Shechem is striking for what it does not say: there is no moral censure of the killing itself, only practical complaint that the violence has made the family politically vulnerable ("I shall be destroyed, I and my house"). The brothers’ retort — "Should he treat our sister as a prostitute?" (34:31) — defends honor; Jacob defends survival. The narrative leaves the moral evaluation to the reader and to Jacob’s deathbed (49:5–7), where Jacob finally pronounces the moral judgment ("cursed be their anger… I will scatter them in Jacob"). The delayed verdict is a Genesis literary signature: moral judgments often arrive chapters or generations after the events, distributed across the canon (Simeon’s eventual absorption into Judah, Lev’s scattering across the tribes). The chapter establishes the principle: actions have consequences that take time to ripen. The Shechem episode’s long aftermath runs through the rest of the patriarchal narrative.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: EDOM, ESAU.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Now these are the generations of Esau, who is Edom'. Ephrem reads the Edom-genealogy as the FAITHFUL recording of the rejected line — Scripture preserves Esau's descendants not to praise but to remember. Tewahedo historiographical tradition preserves the principle: even the rejected names are recorded, because divine memory excludes no one. The Mäṣḥafä Sǝnksar (Tewahedo Synaxarium) preserves names of heretics and apostates in this same spirit — for memory, not for veneration.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BASHEMATH sweet-smelling. (1.) The daughter of Ishmael, the last of Esau’s three wives (Genesis 36:3, 4, 13), from whose son Reuel four tribes of the Edomites sprung. She is also called Mahalath (Genesis 28:9). It is noticeable that Esau’s three wives receive different names in the genealogical table of the Edomites (Genesis 36) from those given to them in the history (Genesis 26:34; 28:9). (2.) A daughter of Solomon, and wife of Ahimaaz, one of his officers (1 Kings 4:15).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: BASHEMATH, ELIPHAZ, REUEL.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ELIPHAZ God his strength. (1.) One of Job’s “three friends” who visited him in his affliction (4:1). He was a “Temanite”, i.e., a native of Teman, in Idumea. He first enters into debate with Job. His language is uniformly more delicate and gentle than that of the other two, although he imputes to Job special sins as the cause of his present sufferings. He states with remarkable force of language the infinite purity and majesty of God (4:12-21; 15:12-16). (2.) The son of Esau by his wife Adah, and father of several Edomitish tribes (Genesis 36:4, 10, 11, 16).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). REUEL friend of God. (1.) A son of Esau and Bashemath (Genesis 36:4, 10; 1 Chronicles 1:35). (2.) “The priest of Midian,” Moses’ father-in-law (Exodus 2:18)=Raguel (Numbers 10:29). If he be identified with Jethro (q.v.), then this may be regarded as his proper name, and Jether or Jethro (i.e., “excellency”) as his official title. (3.) Numbers 2:14, called also Deuel (1:14; 7:42).

↩ ◇ Note. Esau as Edom. The chapter is the OT’s most extended Edomite genealogy, identifying Esau as the eponymous ancestor of Edom — the people who occupied the highlands south and east of the Dead Sea (Mount Seir). The fraternal-rival relationship between Israel and Edom runs through the entire OT: Edomite resistance during the wilderness period (Num 20:14–21), David’s subjugation of Edom (2 Sam 8:13–14), Edom’s opportunistic violence against Judah during the Babylonian destruction (Ps 137:7, Obadiah’s entire prophecy), and the Maccabean-era forced conversion of Idumea (the Greek name for Edom). The chapter’s placement here — extended Edomite genealogy before the resumption of Joseph-cycle narrative in ch 37 — frames the ongoing canonical contrast: Esau’s line becomes a kingdom rapidly (36:31, "before any king reigned over the children of Israel"); Jacob’s line becomes Israel slowly. The chapter’s detail registers the OT’s recurring fascination with the elder-brother lineage: even when not chosen, Esau’s descendants matter, and Genesis preserves their record in detail.

It was noted for the wisdom of its inhabitants (Amos 1:12; Obad. 1:8; Jeremiah 49:7; Ezekiel 25:13). It was divided from the hills of Paran by the low plain of Arabah (Habakkuk 3:3).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KORAH ice, hail. (1.) The third son of Esau, by Aholibamah (Genesis 36:14; 1 Chronicles 1:35). (2.) A Levite, the son of Izhar, the brother of Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:21). The institution of the Aaronic priesthood and the Levitical service at Sinai was a great religious revolution. The old priesthood of the heads of families passed away. This gave rise to murmurings and discontent, while the Israelites were encamped at Kadesh for the first time, which came to a head in a rebellion against Moses and Aaron, headed by Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Two hundred and fifty princes, “men of renown” i.e., well-known men from among the other tribes, joined this conspiracy. The whole company demanded of Moses and Aaron that the old state of things should be restored, alleging that “they took too much upon them” (Numbers 16:1-3). On the morning after the outbreak, Korah and his associates presented themselves at the door of the tabernacle, and “took every man his censer, and put fire in them, and laid incense thereon.” But immediately “fire from the Lord” burst forth and destroyed them all (Numbers 16:35). Dathan and Abiram “came out and stood in the door of their tents, and their wives, and their sons, and their little children,” and it came to pass “that the ground clave asunder that was under them; and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them up.” A plague thereafter began among the people who sympathized in the rebellion, and was only stayed by Aaron’s appearing between the living and the dead, and making “an atonement for the people” (16:47). The descendants of the sons of Korah who did not participate in the rebellion afterwards rose to eminence in the Levitical service.

↩ ◇ Note. The Edomite kings list. The chapter lists eight kings of Edom by name with succession pattern, then tribal chieftains. The introductory formula — "before any king reigned over the children of Israel" — is one of the OT’s strongest internal indicators of post-monarchic dating: the editor is writing from a vantage point at which Israel does have kings, looking back to a period when Edom did but Israel did not. Most modern critical scholarship treats the formula as one of the clearest signals that Genesis as a finished work cannot be earlier than Saul’s reign (the first Israelite king, ca. 1020 BCE), with most placing the final compilation considerably later. The chapter is therefore unusually transparent about its own historical perspective. Theologically, the verse registers a striking observation: Esau’s line organized into stable monarchy long before Jacob’s line did. The OT does not interpret this as Esau’s superiority; rather, monarchy itself is theologically ambivalent in the OT (1 Sam 8). Edom’s precocity in monarchy is, on the deuteronomistic reading, not an advantage but an early symptom of a different political-religious trajectory.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: CIVIL SERVICE, ISHMAELITES, POTIPHAR.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). POTIPHAR dedicated to Ra; i.e., to the sun-God, the Egyptian to whom the Ishmaelites sold Joseph (Genesis 39:1). He was “captain of the guard”, i.e., chief, probably, of the state police, who, while they formed part of the Egyptian army, were also largely employed in civil duties (37:36; marg., “chief of the executioners”). Joseph, though a foreigner, gradually gained his confidence, and became overseer over all his possessions. Believing the false accusation which his profligate wife brought against Joseph, Potiphar cast him into prison, where he remained for some years. (See JOSEPH.)

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s refusal. The verse contains the OT’s most concentrated single articulation of moral integrity under sexual temptation. Joseph’s reasoning is theologically precise: the wrong is not primarily against Potiphar (though Potiphar’s trust would be betrayed), nor against Potiphar’s wife (though she would be implicated in transgression), but "against God." The episode is one of the OT’s clearest demonstrations that ethics is grounded vertically in covenantal relationship before it is grounded horizontally in social obligation. The detail is also narratively significant: Joseph refuses what would be (in ANE court culture) ordinary opportunistic advancement — a powerful patron’s wife’s favor — and pays for the refusal with imprisonment. The chapter’s subsequent vindication theology (39:21–23, Yahweh’s favor in prison) makes the moral framework clear: integrity costs short-term, but Yahweh’s providence eventually reverses the apparent loss. Joseph’s rise to the second highest position in Egypt comes through, not despite, this initial integrity. The episode is one of the OT’s clearest Wisdom-narrative anticipations of the Proverbs theme of righteous suffering vindicated.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?' Ephrem reads Joseph's reasoning as a perfect model of conscience: he refuses on FAITHFULNESS-to-Potiphar AND on faithfulness-to-God. Tewahedo monastic-ethical tradition cites Joseph as the canonical chastity-model: the rejection is reasoned, not just instinctive.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HEBREW a name applied to the Israelites in Scripture only by one who is a foreigner (Genesis 39:14, 17; 41:12, etc.), or by the Israelites when they speak of themselves to foreigners (40:15; Exodus 1:19), or when spoken of an contrasted with other peoples (Genesis 43:32; Exodus 1:3, 7, 15; Deuteronomy 15:12). In the New Testament there is the same contrast between Hebrews and foreigners (Acts 6:1; Phil. 3:5). Derivation. (1.) The name is derived, according to some, from Eber (Genesis 10:24), the ancestor of Abraham. The Hebrews are “sons of Eber” (10:21). (2.) Others trace the name of a Hebrew root-word signifying “to pass over,” and hence regard it as meaning “the man who passed over,” viz., the Euphrates; or to the Hebrew word meaning “the region” or “country beyond,” viz., the land of Chaldea. This latter view is preferred. It is the more probable origin of the designation given to Abraham coming among the Canaanites as a man from beyond the Euphrates (Genesis 14:13). (3.) A third derivation of the word has been suggested, viz., that it is from the Hebrew word ’abhar, “to pass over,” whence ’ebher, in the sense of a “sojourner” or “passer through” as distinct from a “settler” in the land, and thus applies to the condition of Abraham (Hebrews 11:13).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PRISON The first occasion on which we read of a prison is in the history of Joseph in Egypt. Then Potiphar, “Joseph’s master, took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound” (Genesis 39:20-23). The Hebrews word here used (sohar) means properly a round tower or fortress. It seems to have been a part of Potiphar’s house, a place in which state prisoners were kept. The Mosaic law made no provision for imprisonment as a punishment. In the wilderness two persons were “put in ward” (Leviticus 24:12; Numbers 15:34), but it was only till the mind of God concerning them should be ascertained. Prisons and prisoners are mentioned in the book of Psalms (69:33; 79:11; 142:7). Samson was confined in a Philistine prison (Judges 16:21, 25). In the subsequent history of Israel frequent references are made to prisons (1 Kings 22:27; 2 Kings 17:4; 25:27, 29; 2 Chronicles 16:10; Isaiah 42:7; Jeremiah 32:2). Prisons seem to have been common in New Testament times (Matthew 11:2; 25:36, 43). The apostles were put into the “common prison” at the instance of the Jewish council (Acts 5:18, 23; 8:3); and at Philippi Paul and Silas were thrust into the “inner prison” (16:24; comp. 4:3; 12:4, 5).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Afflicted Saints, Egypt, Injustice, Prisons, Prisons.

↩ ◇ Note. "Yahweh was with him." The phrase ("the LORD was with Joseph") forms one of the chapter’s structural refrains, occurring at 39:2, 21, and 23 — bracketing both the rise in Potiphar’s house and the descent into prison. The narrative point is theologically subtle: the same divine presence that made Joseph prosper in Potiphar’s house follows him into the prison and produces favor with the warden there too. Yahweh’s being-with does not exempt Joseph from suffering or false accusation; it operates within those circumstances rather than removing them. The chapter is one of the OT’s sharpest articulations of providence-through-suffering — a theological pattern that becomes structural in OT and NT both (Job, the Servant Songs of Isa 40–55, Christ’s passion). The Joseph cycle as a whole works out this principle at length: every apparent setback (sold into slavery, falsely imprisoned, forgotten by the cupbearer) becomes the necessary precondition for the next stage of his eventual rise to Pharaoh’s second-in-command. The verse is the chapter’s theological center.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BUTLER properly a servant in charge of the wine (Genesis 40:1-13; 41:9). The Hebrew word, mashkeh, thus translated is rendered also (plural) “cup-bearers” (1 Kings 10:5; 2 Chronicles 9:4). Nehemiah (1:11) was cup-bearer to king Artaxerxes. It was a position of great responsibility and honour in royal households.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CUP-BEARER an officer of high rank with Egyptian, Persian, Assyrian, and Jewish monarchs. The cup-bearer of the king of Egypt is mentioned in connection with Joseph’s history (Genesis 40:1-21; 41:9). Rabshakeh (q.v.) was cup-bearer in the Assyrian court (2 Kings 18:17). Nehemiah filled this office to the king of Persia (Nehemiah 1:11). We read also of Solomon’s cup-bearers (1 Kings 10:5; 2 Chronicles 9:4).

↩ ◇ Note. The dream-interpretation principle. Joseph’s answer to the cupbearer and baker — "do not interpretations belong to God?" — establishes the entire theological framework for the dream sequences in chs 40–41. The principle is precise: dream-content comes from God; correct interpretation also comes from God; the human interpreter is merely the divinely enabled mediator. The principle distinguishes Joseph’s practice from professional Egyptian dream-interpreters (Egyptian dream books were extensive, with elaborate symbolic dictionaries; cf. the Chester Beatty dream-papyri). Joseph rejects the technical-professional model in favor of a charismatic-revelational one: each interpretation requires fresh divine illumination. The same principle structures the Daniel narratives (Dan 2:27–28, "no wise men… can show the king the mystery… but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets") and informs the broader OT theology of prophecy as distinct from divination. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest single-line articulations of the prophet-as-vehicle theology that runs through the entire prophetic tradition.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you'. Ephrem treats Joseph's reply to the cupbearer and baker as foundational for the doctrine of divine charism: interpretation of dreams is not a human skill but a divine gift, channelled through specific persons. Tewahedo prophetic-discernment tradition (the monastic discernment-of-spirits charism) traces theologically to this verse: the discerner DOES the interpreting but the interpretation BELONGS to God.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CUP a wine-cup (Genesis 40:11, 21), various forms of which are found on Assyrian and Egyptian monuments. All Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold (1 Kings 10: 21). The cups mentioned in the New Testament were made after Roman and Greek models, and were sometimes of gold (Revelation 17:4). The art of divining by means of a cup was practiced in Egypt (Genesis 44:2-17), and in the East generally. The “cup of salvation” (Psalm 116:13) is the cup of thanksgiving for the great salvation. The “cup of consolation” (Jeremiah 16:7) refers to the custom of friends sending viands and wine to console relatives in mourning (Proverbs 31:6). In 1 Corinthians 10:16, the “cup of blessing” is contrasted with the “cup of devils” (1 Corinthians 10:21). The sacramental cup is the “cup of blessing,” because of blessing pronounced over it (Matthew 26:27; Luke 22:17). The “portion of the cup” (Psalm 11:6; 16:5) denotes one’s condition of life, prosperous or adverse. A “cup” is also a type of sensual allurement (Jeremiah 51:7; Proverbs 23:31; Revelation 17:4). We read also of the “cup of astonishment,” the “cup of trembling,” and the “cup of God’s wrath” (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15; Lamentations 4:21; Ezekiel 23:32; Revelation 16:19; comp. Matthew 26:39, 42; John 18:11). The cup is also the symbol of death (Matthew 16:28; Mark 9:1; Hebrews 2:9).

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s plea. The chapter ends with a small but devastating detail: Joseph’s appeal to the cupbearer to remember him is not honored. "Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him" (40:23). The result is two more years of prison (41:1) before Joseph is finally summoned to interpret Pharaoh’s dream. The forgotten promise is theologically calibrated: had the cupbearer remembered immediately, Joseph would have been freed before Pharaoh’s dream — and the larger providential pattern (Joseph as Pharaoh’s second-in-command, Egypt prepared for famine, the family of Jacob saved) could not have unfolded. The narrative principle: human forgetfulness becomes the medium of divine timing. The chapter is one of the most sophisticated single deferrals in OT narrative — the theological point of two unnecessary prison years is precisely that they are necessary for the providential timeline. The Joseph cycle as a whole works out this pattern of redemptive delay across multiple chapters.

↩ ◇ Note. The brothers’ awakening. Twenty years after selling Joseph into Egyptian slavery, the brothers — confronted by the apparently arbitrary cruelty of "the Egyptian governor" (Joseph in disguise) — recognize their predicament as moral consequence. The Hebrew is striking: "we are guilty (asham) concerning our brother" — the technical legal-ritual word for incurred guilt requiring expiation. The episode is one of the OT’s clearest portraits of long-delayed conscience: the moral reality of an act buried for two decades suddenly emerges in the apparent injustice of a present situation. Joseph, hearing this through an interpreter, has to leave the room to weep (42:24) — the first of his weepings before the brothers in the cycle. The chapter is one of the OT’s sharpest psychological-theological observations: guilt that has been suppressed eventually surfaces, and the surfacing is sometimes triggered by suffering that resembles the suffering originally inflicted. Augustine’s reading of conscience in the Confessions draws explicitly on Joseph-cycle patterns of buried-then-emerging memory.

'And he turned himself about from them, and wept; and returned to them again'. Ephrem treats Joseph's hidden weeping as the model of concealed-compassion: Joseph maintains the testing-disguise BUT the compassion is real and ongoing. Tewahedo pastoral-theology preserves this image: shepherds and confessors may need to maintain apparent severity for the penitent's good, but the compassion underneath must always be active.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s refusal. Jacob’s flat refusal to send Benjamin to Egypt with the brothers — even when the family is starving — registers the depth of his trauma over Joseph: "his brother is dead, and he only is left." The narrator preserves Jacob’s misperception throughout — Jacob assumes Joseph is dead and treats Rachel’s remaining son Benjamin as the last fragile vestige of his beloved wife’s memory. The chapter is one of the OT’s most painfully ironic: the man Jacob refuses to lose Benjamin to is in fact Joseph, the very son Jacob assumes already lost. The Joseph cycle’s entire dramatic structure depends on this irony — the reader knows what Jacob does not, and the suspense across chs 42–45 is generated by the gap. The verse is also significant for what it implies about the dynamics of Jacob’s remaining family: the older sons (sons of Leah, Bilhah, Zilpah) feel themselves expendable in Jacob’s grief, replaceable, ungrieved-for; only Rachel’s sons — Joseph (presumed dead) and Benjamin — receive Jacob’s full attention. The favoritism that drove the brothers to violence in ch 37 has not been corrected.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s second weeping. The Joseph cycle stages four weepings of Joseph before his brothers (42:24, 43:30, 45:2, 46:29, with additional weepings at 50:17 and 50:1 over Jacob’s death). The pattern marks Joseph’s emotional progression toward eventual self-revelation: each weeping is more difficult to conceal, more directly tied to a specific brother (here, Benjamin, whom Joseph has not seen in twenty years). The Hebrew nikhm’ru raḥamav — literally "his bowels grew warm" — uses one of the OT’s strongest somatic-emotional idioms; the inner organs are the seat of compassion in Hebrew anthropology, with the same root behind raḥamim ("compassion, mercies"). The narrative restraint is exquisite: Joseph excuses himself to weep privately, washes his face, controls himself, and returns to the meal as if nothing had happened. The chapter is one of the OT’s most sustained portraits of suppressed emotion controlled across long stretches of public composure. The eventual breaking-point in 45:1–2 is theologically calibrated: when concealment can no longer hold, the truth emerges in tears.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABOMINATION This word is used, (1.) To express the idea that the Egyptians considered themselves as defiled when they ate with strangers (Genesis 43:32). The Jews subsequently followed the same practice, holding it unlawful to eat or drink with foreigners (John 18:28; Acts 10:28; 11:3). (2.) Every shepherd was “an abomination” unto the Egyptians (Genesis 46:34). This aversion to shepherds, such as the Hebrews, arose probably from the fact that Lower and Middle Egypt had formerly been held in oppressive subjection by a tribe of nomad shepherds (the Hyksos), who had only recently been expelled, and partly also perhaps from this other fact that the Egyptians detested the lawless habits of these wandering shepherds. (3.) Pharaoh was so moved by the fourth plague, that while he refused the demand of Moses, he offered a compromise, granting to the Israelites permission to hold their festival and offer their sacrifices in Egypt. This permission could not be accepted, because Moses said they would have to sacrifice “the abomination of the Egyptians” (Exodus 8:26); i.e., the cow or ox, which all the Egyptians held as sacred, and which they regarded it as sacrilegious to kill. (4.) Daniel (11:31), in that section of his prophecies which is generally interpreted as referring to the fearful calamities that were to fall on the Jews in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, says, “And they shall place the abomination that maketh desolate.” Antiochus Epiphanes caused an altar to be erected on the altar of burnt-offering, on which sacrifices were offered to Jupiter Olympus. (Comp. 1 Macc. 1:57). This was the abomination of the desolation of Jerusalem. The same language is employed in Daniel 9:27 (comp. Matthew 24:15), where the reference is probably to the image-crowned standards which the Romans set up at the east gate of the temple (A.D. 70), and to which they paid idolatrous honours. “Almost the entire religion of the Roman camp consisted in worshipping the ensign, swearing by the ensign, and in preferring the ensign before all other gods.” These ensigns were an “abomination” to the Jews, the “abomination of desolation.” This word is also used symbolically of sin in general (Isaiah 66:3); an idol (44:19); the ceremonies of the apostate Church of Rome (Revelation 17:4); a detestable act (Ezekiel 22:11).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EATING The ancient Hebrews would not eat with the Egyptians (Genesis 43:32). In the time of our Lord they would not eat with Samaritans (John 4:9), and were astonished that he ate with publicans and sinners (Matthew 9:11). The Hebrews originally sat at table, but afterwards adopted the Persian and Chaldean practice of reclining (Luke 7:36-50). Their principal meal was at noon (Genesis 43:16; 1 Kings 20:16; Ruth 2:14; Luke 14:12). The word “eat” is used metaphorically in Jeremiah 15:16; Ezekiel 3:1; Revelation 10:9. In John 6:53-58, “eating and drinking” means believing in Christ. Women were never present as guests at meals (q.v.).

↩ ◇ Note. The fivefold portion. Joseph’s deliberate display of favoritism — Benjamin’s portion at the meal is five times larger than the others’ — is one of the chapter’s most theologically loaded details. The narrative suspense is precise: Joseph is testing whether the brothers will resent the favored brother as they once resented him. If they show the same envy that motivated their selling Joseph in ch 37, Joseph will not be able to trust them; if they accept Benjamin’s favor without grievance, the moral repair has happened. The brothers’ silent acceptance ("they drank, and were merry with him") suggests they have changed — the test is implicitly passed. The episode is structural: chs 43–44 are one extended psychological test of the brothers’ moral transformation, with each chapter raising the stakes. The fivefold portion is the test’s opening; the chapter’s closure with the brothers’ unenvious enjoyment of the meal sets up the decisive test of ch 44 (the framing of Benjamin for theft, requiring the brothers to choose whether to abandon him as they once abandoned Joseph).

↩ ◇ Note. Judah’s confession. Confronted with the apparent theft (Joseph’s silver cup planted in Benjamin’s sack), Judah does not protest innocence — he confesses guilt. The "iniquity" he confesses is not the theft (which the brothers did not commit) but the original sin of the cycle: selling Joseph into slavery. The Hebrew matza Elohim et avon ("God has found out the iniquity") is one of the OT’s clearest articulations of the moral principle that long-buried sin eventually surfaces under divine providence. The episode marks Judah’s transformation: the brother who proposed selling Joseph (37:26–27) now offers himself as substitute for Benjamin (44:33), shouldering the punishment that should fall on his half-brother. The Hebrew theology of substitutionary atonement — the willing exchange of one person’s suffering for another’s — finds one of its earliest narrative expressions here. Judah’s offer becomes the trigger for Joseph’s self-revelation in ch 45. The chapter is the moral hinge of the entire Joseph cycle.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Then Judah came near unto him, and said... let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord'. Ephrem reads Judah's offering of himself as substitute for Benjamin as the OT type of Christ's substitutionary atonement: Judah (the tribe of the future Messiah) offers himself FOR another, anticipating the action of his great descendant. Tewahedo Christology preserves this typology as a key OT witness to vicarious atonement.

↩ ◇ Note. Judah’s substitutionary offer. Judah’s offer to remain in Egypt as Joseph’s slave in Benjamin’s place is one of the OT’s most theologically dense single moments. The structure is precisely substitutionary: Judah names the alternative ("when I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us… I shall bear the blame to my father forever," 44:32, 34) and chooses voluntary substitution as the only acceptable resolution. The episode is the moral inverse of ch 37: where the brothers once collectively betrayed Joseph for material gain (twenty pieces of silver), Judah now individually offers himself for Benjamin at total cost. Christian theological tradition has often noted the typological resonance: from the tribe of Judah (cf. 49:8–12), the messianic substitute will come — Christ as offered-substitute is foreshadowed in Judah-as-offered-substitute here. The principle the chapter encodes — voluntary self-substitution as the form moral repair takes — is one of the deepest single theological patterns in the OT, directly echoed by Moses in Exod 32:32 and by the Servant of Isa 53. The verse is the spiritual climax of the cycle.

↩ ◇ Note. The descent to Egypt. Yahweh’s final patriarchal-period theophany — to Jacob at Beersheba, on the way down to Egypt — explicitly authorizes the descent that will be the precondition for the entire exodus narrative. The verse closes the patriarchal phase of the Genesis story: Abraham was called up to Canaan (12:1); Jacob is now sent down to Egypt (46:3). The chiastic geographical movement is theologically deliberate: the family must go down before it can come up as Israel. The promise Yahweh attaches ("there I will make of you a great nation") explicitly identifies Egypt as the place where the Abrahamic promise of nationhood will be fulfilled — Israel becomes a nation in Egyptian slavery, not in Canaanite freedom, theologically registering that nationhood is gift in spite of context, not consequence of context. The chapter’s detail of Jacob’s 70-person family (46:8–27) becomes the baseline against which Exodus 1:7 will register multiplication ("the children of Israel were fruitful and increased abundantly"). The descent that the patriarch fears is the actual mechanism of fulfillment.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JUDAH , TRIBE OF Judah and his three surviving sons went down with Jacob into Egypt (Genesis 46:12; Exodus 1:2). At the time of the Exodus, when we meet with the family of Judah again, they have increased to the number of 74,000 males (Numbers 1:26, 27). Its number increased in the wilderness (26:22). Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, represented the tribe as one of the spies (13:6; 34:19). This tribe marched at the van on the east of the tabernacle (Numbers 2:3-9; 10:14), its standard, as is supposed, being a lion’s whelp. Under Caleb, during the wars of conquest, they conquered that portion of the country which was afterwards assigned to them as their inheritance. This was the only case in which any tribe had its inheritance thus determined (Joshua 14:6-15; 15:13-19). The inheritance of the tribe of Judah was at first fully one-third of the whole country west of Jordan, in all about 2,300 square miles (Joshua 15). But there was a second distribution, when Simeon received an allotment, about 1,000 square miles, out of the portion of Judah (Joshua 19:9). That which remained to Judah was still very large in proportion to the inheritance of the other tribes. The boundaries of the territory are described in Joshua 15:20-63. This territory given to Judah was divided into four sections. (1.) The south (Hebrews negeb), the undulating pasture-ground between the hills and the desert to the south (Joshua 15:21.) This extent of pasture-land became famous as the favourite camping-ground of the old patriarchs. (2.) The “valley” (15:33) or lowland (Hebrews shephelah), a broad strip lying between the central highlands and the Mediterranean. This tract was the garden as well as the granary of the tribe. (3.) The “hill-country,” or the mountains of Judah, an elevated plateau stretching from below Hebron northward to Jerusalem. “The towns and villages were generally perched on the tops of hills or on rocky slopes. The resources of the soil were great. The country was rich in corn, wine, oil, and fruit; and the daring shepherds were able to lead their flocks far out over the neighbouring plains and through the mountains.” The number of towns in this district was thirty-eight (Joshua 15:48-60). (4.) The “wilderness,” the sunken district next the Dead Sea (Joshua 15:61), “averaging 10 miles in breadth, a wild, barren, uninhabitable region, fit only to afford scanty pasturage for sheep and goats, and a secure home for leopards, bears, wild goats, and outlaws” (1 Samuel 17:34; 22:1; Mark 1:13). It was divided into the “wilderness of En-gedi” (1 Samuel 24:1), the “wilderness of Judah” (Judges 1:16; Matthew 3:1), between the Hebron mountain range and the Dead Sea, the “wilderness of Maon” (1 Samuel 23:24). It contained only six cities. Nine of the cities of Judah were assigned to the priests (Joshua 21:9-19).

↩ ◇ Note. The reunion at Goshen. Jacob and Joseph’s reunion — twenty-two years after Joseph was sold into slavery — is one of the OT’s most affecting scenes. The narrator’s vocabulary is precise and economical: Joseph "fell on his neck and wept on his neck a long while" (Hebrew od, "still, longer"). The detail of the prolonged weeping, after twenty-two years of bereavement, registers the depth of grief Jacob carried. Jacob’s reply — "now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive" (46:30) — frames his subsequent seventeen years in Egypt as bonus-time after the unexpected restoration. The chapter completes the structural inversion: Jacob, who once saw Joseph’s blood-soaked coat and concluded "a wild beast has devoured him" (37:33), now sees Joseph alive in Pharaoh’s second-chariot. The narrative arc of grief reversed by recognition — death assumed, life discovered — is one of the OT’s most influential narrative patterns, recurring in resurrection-narrative shapes across the canon. The verse is the formal closure of the Joseph cycle’s primary plot.

↩ ◇ Note. The double adoption. Jacob’s deathbed adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons — counted alongside Reuben and Simeon as full tribal patriarchs — has long-running canonical consequences: the resulting twelve-tribe structure of Israel ends up with two tribes from Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) rather than one (Joseph), with Levi separated from territorial allotment because of priestly status. The bookkeeping math: 12 sons of Jacob, but Levi without territory and Joseph counted twice = the standard 12-tribe territorial list (Reuben, Simeon, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Benjamin, Ephraim, Manasseh). The chapter is also one of the OT’s clearest cases of patriarchal blessing reversing primogeniture: Jacob crosses his hands to put the right-hand blessing on younger Ephraim rather than older Manasseh (48:13–20), repeating the pattern that has run through Genesis (Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph over his older brothers). The verse encodes one of the OT’s structural theological principles: divine election consistently inverts birth-order expectations.

↩ ◇ Note. The reversed blessing. Jacob’s explicit affirmation that the younger Ephraim will surpass the older Manasseh — over Joseph’s objection (48:17–18) — is one of the clearest articulations of the elder-younger reversal that runs through Genesis. The historical fulfillment is unambiguous: Ephraim becomes the dominant northern tribe, sometimes even functioning as a synecdoche for the entire northern kingdom (cf. Hosea’s repeated "Ephraim" for the northern kingdom; Isa 7:9, 17). Manasseh, while territorially large (with both western and trans-Jordanian portions), never produces the political-religious significance of Ephraim. The principle the chapter encodes — younger-over-older as the recurring divine pattern — is theologically consistent with the rest of Genesis but stands in continuous tension with the actual ANE legal-cultural premium on primogeniture. The Genesis pattern is theologically deliberate counter-cultural: the deity does not honor the social hierarchy that the surrounding cultures take for granted, but operates by criteria of grace and choice rather than birth-order. Paul will eventually cite the pattern at Rom 9:10–13 to articulate the same principle theologically.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s prayer. Jacob’s prayer the night before meeting Esau is one of Genesis’s most emotionally exposed moments. The Hebrew opening — qatonti mi-kol ha-ḥasadim, "I am too small for all the loving-kindnesses" — uses an unusual self-diminishing formula that registers genuine humility: Jacob is acknowledging that the prosperity Yahweh has given him exceeds what he deserves. The prayer’s theological structure is exemplary: invocation of Yahweh as covenant-God of his fathers (32:9), self-abasement (32:10), specific request for protection (32:11), and appeal to divine promise (32:12). The chapter overall is one of the OT’s most carefully constructed sequences: Jacob’s elaborate gifts to Esau (32:13–21), the dispatch of his family across the Jabbok (32:22–23), and finally the all-night wrestling-match with the divine figure (32:24–32). The prayer functions as the chapter’s pivot — Jacob has to come to grips with his own inadequacy before he can face either Esau or the night-stranger. The verse encodes one of the OT’s clearest portraits of authentic prayer.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Yisra’el (יִשְׂרָאֵל). Jacob’s name-change is reaffirmed here at Bethel after first being given at the Jabbok (32:28). The doubled naming registers narrative weight: this is a permanent identity-shift, not a momentary epithet. The Hebrew etymology offered at 32:28 — "you have striven (sarita) with God and with men, and have prevailed" — produces "Israel" as "one who strives with God" or "God strives." The name will become both the patriarch’s personal name (used interchangeably with "Jacob" through the rest of Genesis) and the entire people’s designation. The principle the renaming encodes — identity through encounter rather than birth — runs through the rest of OT theology: covenant-naming creates community where biology alone could not. The verse is also the chapter’s key theological moment: Bethel ("house of God") becomes the site where the patriarch’s new identity is formally divinely confirmed, not just won wrestling. The chapter establishes Bethel as one of the major patriarchal cultic sites — later abused by Jeroboam’s northern calf-cult (1 Kgs 12:28–33) and condemned by Amos (Amos 4:4, "go to Bethel and transgress").

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it his brethren, and said, Behold, I have dreamed a dream more; and, behold, the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me'. Ephrem reads Joseph's astral dream as a Marian prefiguration: Rev 12:1 ('a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars') reuses Joseph's imagery for Mary. Tewahedo Marian iconography preserves the Rev-12 crown imagery, reading Joseph's dream as the OT root.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). STARS The eleven stars (Genesis 37:9); the seven (Amos 5:8); wandering (Jude 1:13); seen in the east at the birth of Christ, probably some luminous meteors miraculously formed for this specific purpose (Matthew 2:2-10); stars worshipped (Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 17:16; 21:3; Jeremiah 19:13); spoken of symbolically (Numbers 24:17; Revelation 1:16, 20; 12:1). (See ASTROLOGERS.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DOTHAN two wells, a famous pasture-ground where Joseph found his brethren watching their flocks. Here, at the suggestion of Judah, they sold him to the Ishmaelite merchants (Genesis 37:17). It is mentioned on monuments in B.C. 1600. It was the residence of Elisha (2 Kings 6:13), and the scene of a remarkable vision of chariots and horses of fire surrounding the mountain on which the city stood. It is identified with the modern Tell-Dothan, on the south side of the plain of Jezreel, about 12 miles north of Samaria, among the hills of Gilboa. The “two wells” are still in existence, one of which bears the name of the “pit of Joseph” (Jubb Yusuf).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BALM contracted from Bal’sam, a general name for many oily or resinous substances which flow or trickle from certain trees or plants when an incision is made through the bark. (1.) This word occurs in the Authorized Version (Genesis 37:25; 43:11; Jeremiah 8:22; 46:11; 51:8; Ezekiel 27:17) as the rendering of the Hebrew word tsori or tseri, which denotes the gum of a tree growing in Gilead (q.v.), which is very precious. It was celebrated for its medicinal qualities, and was circulated as an article of merchandise by Arab and Phoenician merchants. The shrub so named was highly valued, and was almost peculiar to Palestine. In the time of Josephus it was cultivated in the neighbourhood of Jericho and the Dead Sea. There is an Arab tradition that the tree yielding this balm was brought by the queen of Sheba as a present to Solomon, and that he planted it in his gardens at Jericho. (2.) There is another Hebrew word, basam or bosem, from which our word “balsam,” as well as the corresponding Greek balsamon, is derived. It is rendered “spice” (Cant. 5:1, 13; 6:2; margin of Revised Version, “balsam;” Exodus 35:28; 1 Kings 10:10), and denotes fragrance in general. Basam also denotes the true balsam-plant, a native of South Arabia (Cant. l.c.).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GILEAD , BALM OF The region of Gilead abounded in spices and aromatic gums, which were exported to Egypt and Tyre (Genesis 37:25; Jeremiah 8:22; 46:11; Ezekiel 27:17). The word “balm” is a contracted form of “balsam,” a word derived from the Greek balsamon, which was adopted as the representative of the Hebrew words baal shemen, meaning “Lord” or “chief of oils.” The Hebrew name of this balm was tsori. The tree yielding this medicinal oil was probably the Balsamodendron opobalsamum of botanists, and the Amyris opobalsamum of Linnaeus. It is an evergreen, rising to the height of about 14 feet. The oil or resin, exuding through an orifice made in its bark in very small quantities, is esteemed of great value for its supposed medicinal qualities. (See BALM.) It may be noted that Coverdale’s version reads in Jeremiah 8:22, “There is no triacle in Galaad.” The word “triacle” = “treacle” is used in the sense of ointment.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MERCHANT The Hebrew word so rendered is from a root meaning “to travel about,” “to migrate,” and hence “a traveller.” In the East, in ancient times, merchants travelled about with their merchandise from place to place (Genesis 37:25; Job 6:18), and carried on their trade mainly by bartering (Genesis 37:28; 39:1). After the Hebrews became settled in Palestine they began to engage in commercial pursuits, which gradually expanded (49:13; Deuteronomy 33:18; Judges 5:17), till in the time of Solomon they are found in the chief marts of the world (1 Kings 9:26; 10:11, 26, 28; 22:48; 2 Chronicles 1:16; 9:10, 21). After Solomon’s time their trade with foreign nations began to decline. After the Exile it again expanded into wider foreign relations, because now the Jews were scattered in many lands.

↩ ◇ Note. The sale price. Twenty shekels of silver was the standard price of a young male slave in ANE slave-markets of the Middle Bronze Age — attested in the Code of Hammurabi (§116) and in Mesopotamian and Egyptian commercial records. The narrative detail is precisely period-appropriate; later periods saw slave-prices rise (Lev 27:5 sets the dedication-redemption value of a male 5–20 years old at 20 shekels; Exod 21:32 sets the gore-by-ox compensation for a slave at 30 shekels in a slightly later period). The verse is one of the OT’s small windows on the actual slave-market economics of the patriarchal era, and the price’s historical accuracy is one of several details supporting an early second-millennium-BCE date for the underlying tradition. The Christological echo — Judas’ betrayal price of thirty pieces of silver (Matt 26:15, also citing Zech 11:12–13) — has been read as deliberate intertextual signaling: Judas selling Jesus parallels the brothers selling Joseph, who was their predecessor as righteous-sufferer-vindicated. The verse is the moment the entire Joseph-cycle plot turns on.

LEVIRATE LAW from Latin levir, “a husband’s brother,” the name of an ancient custom ordained by Moses, by which, when an Israelite died without issue, his surviving brother was required to marry the widow, so as to continue his brother’s family through the son that might be born of that marriage (Genesis 38:8; Deuteronomy 25:5-10; comp. Ruth 3; 4:10). Its object was “to raise up seed to the departed brother.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). RING Used as an ornament to decorate the fingers, arms, wrists, and also the ears and the nose. Rings were used as a signet (Genesis 38:18). They were given as a token of investment with authority (Genesis 41:42; Esther 3:8-10; 8:2), and of favour and dignity (Luke 15:22). They were generally worn by rich men (James 2:2). They are mentioned by Isiah (3:21) among the adornments of Hebrew women.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SEAL commonly a ring engraved with some device (Genesis 38:18, 25). Jezebel “wrote letters in Ahab’s name, and sealed them with his seal” (1 Kings 21:8). Seals are frequently mentioned in Jewish history (Deuteronomy 32:34; Nehemiah 9:38; 10:1; Esther 3:12; Cant. 8:6; Isaiah 8:16; Jeremiah 22:24; 32:44, etc.). Sealing a document was equivalent to the signature of the owner of the seal. “The use of a signet-ring by the monarch has recently received a remarkable illustration by the discovery of an impression of such a signet on fine clay at Koyunjik, the site of the ancient Nineveh. ANCIENT JEWISH SEALS This seal appears to have been impressed from the bezel of a metallic finger-ring. It is an oval, 2 inches in length by 1 inch wide, and bears the image, name, and titles of the Egyptian king Sabaco” (Rawlinson’s Hist. Illus. of the O.T., p. 46). The actual signet-rings of two Egyptian kings (Cheops and Horus) have been discovered. (See SIGNET.) The use of seals is mentioned in the New Testament only in connection with the record of our Lord’s burial (Matthew 27:66). The tomb was sealed by the Pharisees and chief priests for the purpose of making sure that the disciples would not come and steal the body away (ver. 63, 64). The mode of doing this was probably by stretching a cord across the stone and sealing it at both ends with sealing-clay. When God is said to have sealed the Redeemer, the meaning is, that he has attested his divine mission (John 6:27). Circumcision is a seal, an attestation of the covenant (Romans 4:11). Believers are sealed with the Spirit, as God’s mark put upon them (Ephesians 1:13; 4:30). Converts are by Paul styled the seal of his apostleship, i.e., they are its attestation (1 Corinthians 9:2). Seals and sealing are frequently mentioned in the book of Revelation (5:1; 6:1; 7:3; 10:4; 22:10).

↩ ◇ Note. Judah’s admission. Tamar’s pregnancy by her father-in-law Judah — through her successful disguise as a prostitute when Judah had failed to give her his third son in levirate marriage — is one of the OT’s most morally complex sub-narratives. Judah’s confession ("she is more righteous than I") acknowledges what the chapter has been building: Tamar’s desperate scheme is theologically vindicated as the proper claim on levirate-obligation that Judah was failing to honor. The episode is structurally important: the chapter is inserted into the Joseph cycle (interrupting the seamless narrative between 37:36 and 39:1) for theological reasons. From this Tamar-Judah union come Perez and Zerah (38:29–30), and from Perez descends the Davidic line (Ruth 4:18–22, 1 Chr 2:5–15). Tamar becomes one of the four named women in the genealogy of Christ (Matt 1:3) — alongside Rahab, Ruth, and "the wife of Uriah." The chapter is the OT’s clearest demonstration that the messianic line runs through morally complex circumstances rather than around them. The verse is the canonical vindication of Tamar’s righteousness.

↩ ◇ Note. The Egyptian dream-interpreters. Pharaoh’s court magicians and wise men (Hebrew ḥartummim, the same vocabulary used in Exod 7:11 for Pharaoh’s sorcerers in the plague narratives) cannot interpret his dream — making the stage clear for Joseph’s charismatic-revelational alternative (41:16, "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer"). Egyptian dream-interpretation was a sophisticated professional discipline, with extensive symbolic dictionaries (cf. the Chester Beatty dream-papyri); their failure here is therefore narratively pointed rather than incidental. The same pattern recurs structurally at Dan 2 (the Babylonian wise men cannot interpret Nebuchadnezzar’s dream), Dan 5 (the Babylonian wise men cannot read the writing on the wall) — both echoing this Joseph-cycle pattern: foreign professional divination fails where Israelite charismatic-revelation succeeds. The chapter is the textual prototype for the wisdom-narrative pattern in which Hebrew protagonists exceed foreign court-experts in their own area of professional competence.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Joseph said unto his brethren, I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?' Ephrem reads the self-revelation as the model of merciful self-disclosure: the brothers, expecting wrath, hear MERCY first. Tewahedo theological-anthropology preserves this pattern: divine self-disclosure in Christ runs ahead of and overwhelms human expectation of judgment. The risen Christ's 'Peace be unto you' to the apostles who abandoned Him is the Joseph-pattern fulfilled.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s providence theology. The verse — paired with 50:20 ("you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good") — gives the most concentrated articulation of OT providence theology in the entire canon. The brothers’ act remains evil (the verse does not exonerate them); Yahweh’s overruling sovereignty has nonetheless used their evil for redemptive purposes. The two-level theology — human responsibility for moral choices preserved alongside divine sovereignty over outcomes — becomes one of the OT’s structural theological positions, recurring in Isa 10:5–7 (Assyria as Yahweh’s rod for judgment, but accountable for its own arrogance), Acts 2:23 (Christ "delivered up by the determinate counsel of God" but crucified by "wicked hands"), and Rom 8:28 ("all things work together for good"). The chapter is the OT’s clearest single articulation of the theological framework that holds providence and moral responsibility together without collapsing either. Joseph does not rationalize the brothers’ act; he reads it within a larger frame of divine purpose.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob before Pharaoh. Jacob’s self-description to Pharaoh — "the years of my pilgrimage" (Hebrew m’gurai, "sojournings") — uses the same root that defines patriarchal life as a whole: ger, the resident alien who lives in a land not his own. The patriarchs are "sojourners" in Canaan even though Yahweh has promised them the land; the eschatological fulfillment of land-possession remains future. Heb 11:9–13 picks up exactly this language: "By faith he sojourned (parōikēsen) in the land of promise as in a strange country… they confessed that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth." The verse becomes the OT root of one of the NT’s most powerful spiritual metaphors: the people of God as pilgrims, never fully at home in any earthly arrangement. Jacob’s self-description as having had "few and evil" days (47:9) registers a sober realism about his own life — he does not romanticize the wandering, even as the theological frame retains its dignity. The verse is one of the OT’s most poignant patriarchal self-assessments.

'The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be'. Ephrem reads this as the most explicit messianic prophecy in Genesis: Shiloh = the one to whom (Hebrew shelo = 'his') everything belongs / the one who is sent. Tewahedo Christology preserves the Shiloh-as-Christ identification load-bearingly: the Tewahedo qǝddase explicitly cites Gen 49:10 as proof-text for Christ's Judahic descent and universal lordship ('unto him shall the gathering of the people be').

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NATIVITY OF CHRIST The birth of our Lord took place at the time and place predicted by the prophets (Genesis 49:10; Isaiah 7:14; Jeremiah 31:15; Micah 5:2; Hag. 2:6-9; Daniel 9:24, 25). Joseph and Mary were providentially led to go up to Bethlehem at this period, and there Christ was born (Matthew 2:1, 6; Luke 2:1, 7). The exact year or month or day of his birth cannot, however, now be exactly ascertained. We know, however, that it took place in the “fulness of the time” (Galatians 4:4), i.e., at the fittest time in the world’s history. Chronologists are now generally agreed that the year 4 before the Christian era was the year of Christ’s nativity, and consequently that he was about four years old in the year 1 A.D.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SCEPTRE (Hebrews shebet = Gr. skeptron), properly a staff or rod. As a symbol of authority, the use of the sceptre originated in the idea that the ruler was as a shepherd of his people (Genesis 49:10; Numbers 24:17; Psalm 45:6; Isaiah 14:5). There is no example on record of a sceptre having ever been actually handled by a Jewish king.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SHILOH generally understood as denoting the Messiah, “the peaceful one,” as the word signifies (Genesis 49:10). The Vulgate Version translates the word, “he who is to be sent,” in allusion to the Messiah; the Revised Version, margin, “till he come to Shiloh;” and the LXX., “until that which is his shall come to Shiloh.” It is most simple and natural to render the expression, as in the Authorized Version, “till Shiloh come,” interpreting it as a proper name (comp. Isaiah 9:6). Shiloh, a place of rest, a city of Ephraim, “on the north side of Bethel,” from which it is distant 10 miles (Judges 21:19); the modern Seilun (the Arabic for Shiloh), a “mass of shapeless ruins.” Here the tabernacle was set up after the Conquest (Joshua 18:1-10), where it remained during all the period of the judges till the ark fell into the hands of the Philistines. “No spot in Central Palestine could be more secluded than this early sanctuary, nothing more featureless than the landscape around; so featureless, indeed, the landscape and so secluded the spot that from the time of St. Jerome till its re-discovery by Dr. Robinson in 1838 the very site was forgotten and unknown.” It is referred to by Jeremiah (7:12, 14; 26:4-9) five hundred years after its destruction.
