↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). COLOUR The subject of colours holds an important place in the Scriptures. White occurs as the translation of various Hebrew words. It is applied to milk (Genesis 49:12), manna (Exodus 16:31), snow (Isaiah 1:18), horses (Zechariah 1:8), raiment (Ecclesiastes 9:8). Another Hebrew word so rendered is applied to marble (Esther 1:6), and a cognate word to the lily (Cant. 2:16). A different term, meaning “dazzling,” is applied to the countenance (Cant. 5:10). This colour was an emblem of purity and innocence (Mark 16:5; John 20:12; Revelation 19:8, 14), of joy (Ecclesiastes 9:8), and also of victory (Zechariah 6:3; Revelation 6:2). The hangings of the tabernacle court (Exodus 27:9; 38:9), the coats, mitres, bonnets, and breeches of the priests (Exodus 39:27,28), and the dress of the high priest on the day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:4,32), were white. Black, applied to the hair (Leviticus 13:31; Cant. 5:11), the complexion (Cant. 1:5), and to horses (Zechariah 6:2,6). The word rendered “brown” in Genesis 30:32 (R.V., “black”) means properly “scorched”, i.e., the colour produced by the influence of the sun’s rays. “Black” in Job 30:30 means dirty, blackened by sorrow and disease. The word is applied to a mourner’s robes (Jeremiah 8:21; 14:2), to a clouded sky (1 Kings 18:45), to night (Micah 3:6; Jeremiah 4:28), and to a brook rendered turbid by melted snow (Job 6:16). It is used as symbolical of evil in Zechariah 6:2, 6 and Revelation 6:5. It was the emblem of mourning, affliction, calamity (Jeremiah 14:2; Lamentations 4:8; 5:10). Red, applied to blood (2 Kings 3;22), a heifer (Numbers 19:2), pottage of lentils (Genesis 25:30), a horse (Zechariah 1:8), wine (Proverbs 23:31), the complexion (Genesis 25:25; Cant. 5:10). This colour is symbolical of bloodshed (Zechariah 6:2; Revelation 6:4; 12:3). Purple, a colour obtained from the secretion of a species of shell-fish (the Murex trunculus) which was found in the Mediterranean, and particularly on the coasts of Phoenicia and Asia Minor. The colouring matter in each separate shell-fish amounted to only a single drop, and hence the great value of this dye. Robes of this colour were worn by kings (Judges 8:26) and high officers (Esther 8:15). They were also worn by the wealthy and luxurious (Jeremiah 10:9; Ezekiel 27:7; Luke 16:19; Revelation 17:4). With this colour was associated the idea of royalty and majesty (Judges 8:26; Cant. 3:10; 7:5; Daniel 5:7, 16,29). Blue. This colour was also procured from a species of shell-fish, the chelzon of the Hebrews, and the Helix ianthina of modern naturalists. The tint was emblematic of the sky, the deep dark hue of the Eastern sky. This colour was used in the same way as purple. The ribbon and fringe of the Hebrew dress were of this colour (Numbers 15:38). The loops of the curtains (Exodus 26:4), the lace of the high priest’s breastplate, the robe of the ephod, and the lace on his mitre, were blue (Exodus 28:28, 31, 37). Scarlet, or Crimson. In Isaiah 1:18 a Hebrew word is used which denotes the worm or grub whence this dye was procured. In Genesis 38:28,30, the word so rendered means “to shine,” and expresses the brilliancy of the colour. The small parasitic insects from which this dye was obtained somewhat resembled the cochineal which is found in Eastern countries. It is called by naturalists Coccus ilics. The dye was procured from the female grub alone. The only natural object to which this colour is applied in Scripture is the lips, which are likened to a scarlet thread (Cant. 4:3). Scarlet robes were worn by the rich and luxurious (2 Samuel 1:24; Proverbs 31:21; Jeremiah 4:30. Revelation 17:4). It was also the hue of the warrior’s dress (Nah. 2:3; Isaiah 9:5). The Phoenicians excelled in the art of dyeing this colour (2 Chronicles 2:7). These four colours--white, purple, blue, and scarlet--were used in the textures of the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1, 31, 36), and also in the high priest’s ephod, girdle, and breastplate (Exodus 28:5, 6, 8, 15). Scarlet thread is mentioned in connection with the rites of cleansing the leper (Leviticus 14:4, 6, 51) and of burning the red heifer (Numbers 19:6). It was a crimson thread that Rahab was to bind on her window as a sign that she was to be saved alive (Joshua 2:18; 6:25) when the city of Jericho was taken. Vermilion, the red sulphuret of mercury, or cinnabar; a colour used for drawing the figures of idols on the walls of temples (Ezekiel 23:14), or for decorating the walls and beams of houses (Jeremiah 22:14).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SHIPS early used in foreign commerce by the Phoenicians (Genesis 49:13). Moses (Deuteronomy 28:68) and Job (9:26) make reference to them, and Balaam speaks of the “ships of Chittim” (Numbers 24:24). Solomon constructed a navy at Ezion-geber by the assistance of Hiram’s sailors (1 Kings 9:26-28; 2 Chronicles 8:18). Afterwards, Jehoshaphat sought to provide himself with a navy at the same port, but his ships appear to have been wrecked before they set sail (1 Kings 22:48, 49; 2 Chronicles 20:35-37). In our Lord’s time fishermen’s boats on the Sea of Galilee were called “ships.” Much may be learned regarding the construction of ancient merchant ships and navigation from the record in Acts 27, 28.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SERPENT (Hebrews nahash; Gr. ophis), frequently noticed in Scripture. More than forty species are found in Syria and Arabia. The poisonous character of the serpent is alluded to in Jacob’s blessing on Dan (Genesis 49:17; see Proverbs 30:18, 19; James 3:7; Jeremiah 8:17). (See ADDER.) This word is used symbolically of a deadly, subtle, malicious enemy (Luke 10:19). The serpent is first mentioned in connection with the history of the temptation and fall of our first parents (Genesis 3). It has been well remarked regarding this temptation: “A real serpent was the agent of the temptation, as is plain from what is said of the natural characteristic of the serpent in the first verse of the chapter (3:1), and from the curse pronounced upon the animal itself. But that Satan was the actual tempter, and that he used the serpent merely as his instrument, is evident (1) from the nature of the transaction; for although the serpent may be the most subtle of all the beasts of the field, yet he has not the high intellectual faculties which the tempter here displayed. (2.) In the New Testament it is both directly asserted and in various forms assumed that Satan seduced our first parents into sin (John 8:44; Romans 16:20; 2 Corinthians 11:3, 14; Revelation 12:9; 20:2).” Hodge’s System. Theol., ii. 127.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NAPHTALI , TRIBE OF On this tribe Jacob pronounced the patriarchal blessing, “Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words” (Genesis 49:21). It was intended thus to set forth under poetic imagery the future character and history of the tribe. At the time of the Exodus this tribe numbered 53,400 adult males (Numbers 1:43), but at the close of the wanderings they numbered only 45,400 (26:48-50). Along with Dan and Asher they formed “the camp of Dan,” under a common standard (2:25-31), occupying a place during the march on the north side of the tabernacle. The possession assigned to this tribe is set forth in Joshua 19:32-39. It lay in the north-eastern corner of the land, bounded on the east by the Jordan and the lakes of Merom and Galilee, and on the north it extended far into Coele-Syria, the valley between the two Lebanon ranges. It comprehended a greater variety of rich and beautiful scenery and of soil and climate than fell to the lot of any other tribe. The territory of Naphtali extended to about 800 square miles, being the double of that of Issachar. The region around Kedesh, one of its towns, was originally called Galil, a name afterwards given to the whole northern division of Canaan. A large number of foreigners settled here among the mountains, and hence it was called “Galilee of the Gentiles” (q.v.), Matthew 4:15, 16. The southern portion of Naphtali has been called the “Garden of Palestine.” It was of unrivalled fertility. It was the principal scene of our Lord’s public ministry. Here most of his parables were spoken and his miracles wrought. This tribe was the first to suffer from the invasion of Benhadad, king of Syria, in the reigns of Baasha, king of Israel, and Asa, king of Judah (1 Kings 15:20; 2 Chronicles 16:4). In the reign of Pekah, king of Israel, the Assyrians under Tiglath-pileser swept over the whole north of Israel, and carried the people into captivity (2 Kings 15:29). Thus the kingdom of Israel came to an end (B.C. 722). Naphtali is now almost wholly a desert, the towns of Tiberias, on the shore of the Lake of Galilee, and Safed being the only places in it of any importance.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WOLF Hebrews zeeb, frequently referred to in Scripture as an emblem of treachery and cruelty. Jacob’s prophecy, “Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf” (Genesis 49:27), represents the warlike character of that tribe (see Judges 19-21). Isaiah represents the peace of Messiah’s kingdom by the words, “The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb” (Isaiah 11:6). The habits of the wolf are described in Jeremiah 5:6; Habakkuk 1:8; Zephaniah 3:3; Ezekiel 22:27; Matthew 7:15; 10:16; Acts 20:29. Wolves are still sometimes found in Palestine, and are the dread of shepherds, as of old.

↩ ◇ Note. The patriarchal burial. Jacob’s deathbed instruction connects the entire patriarchal narrative to its physical center: the cave of Machpelah at Hebron, purchased by Abraham in ch 23. The cave eventually receives all three patriarchs, three of the four matriarchs (Rebekah, Leah, and Sarah; Rachel was buried separately near Bethlehem, 35:19), and is held by Jewish tradition to remain the patriarchal-matriarchal burial ground today (the Tomb of the Patriarchs at Hebron, with both Jewish synagogue and Muslim mosque elements, is one of the most contested holy sites in the modern Holy Land). Jacob’s insistence on burial in Canaan — despite dying in Egypt — reflects the patriarchal theology of covenant-land: even when the family is in Egyptian residence, the burial-ground signals where they belong eschatologically. Joseph’s parallel deathbed instruction (50:25, that his bones be carried back to Canaan) is a similar gesture, eventually fulfilled in Josh 24:32. The chapter and Joseph’s parallel make burial-place itself a confession of covenant identity.

↩ ◇ Note. The Egyptian embalming. Jacob receives full Egyptian embalming — a 40-day process (50:3) followed by 70 days of mourning. The detail is historically significant: the patriarchal family at this stage is sufficiently integrated into Egyptian elite society that Jacob receives the kind of mortuary treatment normally reserved for high-status Egyptians. Egyptian embalming required specialist priests with specific ritual-religious dimensions (the embalmers worked under priestly direction, with elaborate prayers to Anubis); the OT does not specify whether the embalmers’ ritual elements were performed for Jacob, but the basic procedure is unambiguous. The chapter is one of Genesis’s most syncretistically realistic about the Egyptian context — Joseph and his family operate within Egyptian institutional frameworks even while preserving Israelite distinctiveness. The 70 days of mourning approximates the Egyptian standard royal mourning period; Pharaoh himself accords Jacob royal-level recognition (50:7, the mourning party including "all the elders of the land of Egypt"). The verse is one of the OT’s clearest pictures of patriarchal-Egyptian interaction at its most elaborate institutional moment.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s lie. Jacob’s direct lie — “I am Esau your firstborn” — is unambiguous. Genesis presents the deception without explicit moral comment, leaving the ethical evaluation to readers and later tradition. Rabbinic readings (Bereshit Rabbah 65:18) sometimes defend Jacob (the blessing was already promised him at 25:23); Christian patristic readings (Augustine, Contra Mendacium) treat it as licit deception within providential plan. Critical readers see the chapter as morally complex theology — God’s elect is also genuinely deceitful, the line of promise is not the line of moral excellence.

↩ ◇ Note. Voice and hands. Isaac’s blind sense-perception splits — voice says Jacob, hands say Esau — and he chooses the wrong evidence. The phrase has become proverbial for hidden identity beneath external appearance. Patristic exegesis (Augustine) read it ecclesiologically: the voice is the church’s, the hands are the worldly disguise. Rabbinic tradition (Bereshit Rabbah 65:20) sees the verse as the structural key to Jewish history: Israel’s voice (prayer, Torah) gives life when Esau’s hands (violence, empire) prevail. The visual-tactile split frames a recurring theme in biblical theology: divine identification often inverts surface appearance.

↩ ◇ Note. Isaac’s trembling. The Hebrew vayecharad…charadah gedolah ʿad-meʾod uses cognate intensification — “he trembled a great trembling, exceedingly” — the strongest emotional vocabulary in the Hebrew Bible. The trembling is not anger but holy dread: Isaac recognizes that providence has overruled his preferred choice. His response — “yes, and he shall be blessed” — affirms Jacob’s blessing rather than revoking it. The patriarchal blessing, once spoken, is irrevocable. The theology of irrevocable speech-act underlies prophetic theology (Isa 55:11; Heb 6:18).

↩ ◇ Note. Esau’s bitter cry. Esau’s tseʿaqah gedolah u-marah ʿad-meʾod is a strikingly intense lament — the same vocabulary used elsewhere of national mourning (Esther 4:1) and of Israel’s cry under bondage (Ex 3:7). Hebrews 12:17 cites this verse as paradigm of irreversible loss: “he was rejected, for he found no place to repent, though he sought it with tears.” The juxtaposition is theologically severe — Esau weeps but cannot reverse. The verse has shaped Christian theology of unforgivable opportunity, though the original Hebrew context is regret over lost blessing rather than damnation.

↩ ◇ Note. One blessing only? Esau’s question reveals the patriarchal blessing’s ontology: a definite, finite act of speech rather than an indefinitely renewable wish. Once Jacob received the blessing of headship and dominion, Isaac had no comparable blessing to give Esau. The lesser blessing he eventually gives (27:39–40) is not equivalent. The economy of blessing — finite, transferable, irrevocable — undergirds the firstborn-displacement pattern in Genesis (Cain/Abel/Seth, Ishmael/Isaac, Esau/Jacob, Manasseh/Ephraim). The chosen line is not the natural firstborn but the one who receives the irreplaceable word.

↩ ◇ Note. The stone pillow. Jacob’s stone-pillow at Bethel becomes one of the patriarchal narrative’s most concrete details. Rabbinic tradition (b. Chullin 91b) develops the stone into a single rock combining many — the foundation stone of the Temple, located at Mount Moriah. Folklore and pilgrimage tradition identifies the stone with the Stone of Scone, used in coronation of Scottish and English monarchs since the 13th century — a tradition asserting Israelite-Davidic descent of British royalty. The literal stone-pillow simply marks Jacob’s vulnerable solitude and unconscious encounter with the holy.

↩ ◇ Note. The standing stone. Jacob’s stone-pillar (matzevah) marks the site as sacred. Standing stones (matzevot) were a widespread ANE religious feature, attested archaeologically at many cult sites in Canaan. The Mosaic law later prohibits them (Deut 16:22; Lev 26:1) precisely because of their Canaanite cultic associations — but Jacob’s pillar predates the prohibition. The oil-anointing transforms a stone into a covenant-marker, the gesture of consecration that gives the Hebrew word mashiach (anointed) its meaning. The site is renamed Beit El — “house of God.”

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: ANOINTING, BETH-EL, JACOB, JACOB, PILLAR.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). STONE Stones were commonly used for buildings, also as memorials of important events (Genesis 28:18; Joshua 24:26, 27; 1 Samuel 7:12, etc.). They were gathered out of cultivated fields (Isaiah 5:2; comp. 2 Kings 3:19). This word is also used figuratively of believers (1 Peter 2:4, 5), and of the Messiah (Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 28:16; Matthew 21:42; Acts 4:11, etc.). In Daniel 2:45 it refers also to the Messiah. He is there described as “cut out of the mountain.” (See ROCK.) A “heart of stone” denotes great insensibility (1 Samuel 25:37). Stones were set up to commemorate remarkable events, as by Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:18), at Padan-aram (35:4), and on the occasion of parting with Laban (31:45-47); by Joshua at the place on the banks of the Jordan where the people first “lodged” after crossing the river (Joshua 6:8), and also in “the midst of Jordan,” where he erected another set of twelve stones (4:1-9); and by Samuel at “Ebenezer” (1 Samuel 7:12).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Anointing, Sacred, Denunciations against, Morning, Pillars, Pillars.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: BETH-EL, JACOB, JACOB, RELIGION, STONES.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BETHEL house of God. (1.) A place in Central Palestine, about 10 miles north of Jerusalem, at the head of the pass of Michmash and Ai. It was originally the royal Canaanite city of Luz (Genesis 28:19). The name Bethel was at first apparently given to the sanctuary in the neighbourhood of Luz, and was not given to the city itself till after its conquest by the tribe of Ephraim. When Abram entered Canaan he formed his second encampment between Bethel and Hai (Genesis 12:8); and on his return from Egypt he came back to it, and again “called upon the name of the Lord” (13:4). Here Jacob, on his way from Beersheba to Haran, had a vision of the angels of God ascending and descending on the ladder whose top reached unto heaven (28:10, 19); and on his return he again visited this place, “where God talked with him” (35:1-15), and there he “built an altar, and called the place El-beth-el” (q.v.). To this second occasion of God’s speaking with Jacob at Bethel, Hosea (12:4,5) makes reference. In troublous times the people went to Bethel to ask counsel of God (Judges 20:18, 31; 21:2). Here the ark of the covenant was kept for a long time under the care of Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron (20:26-28). Here also Samuel held in rotation his court of justice (1 Samuel 7:16). It was included in Israel after the kingdom was divided, and it became one of the seats of the worship of the golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-33; 13:1). Hence the prophet Hosea (Hos. 4:15; 5:8; 10:5, 8) calls it in contempt Beth-aven, i.e., “house of idols.” Bethel remained an abode of priests even after the kingdom of Israel was desolated by the king of Assyria (2 Kings 17:28, 29). At length all traces of the idolatries were extirpated by Josiah, king of Judah (2 Kings 23:15-18); and the place was still in existence after the Captivity (Ezra 2:28; Nehemiah 7:32). It has been identified with the ruins of Beitin, a small village amid extensive ruins some 9 miles south of Shiloh. (2.) Mount Bethel was a hilly district near Bethel (Joshua 16:1; 1 Samuel 13:2). (3.) A town in the south of Judah (Joshua 8:17; 12:16).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LUZ a nut-bearing tree, the almond. (1.) The ancient name of a royal Canaanitish city near the site of Bethel (Genesis 28:19; 35:6), on the border of Benjamin (Joshua 18:13). Here Jacob halted, and had a prophetic vision. (See BETHEL.) (2.) A place in the land of the Hittites, founded (Judges 1:26) by “a man who came forth out of the city of Luz.” It is identified with Luweiziyeh, 4 miles north-west of Banias.

↩ ◇ Note. The first explicit human vow. Jacob’s vow (neder) is the first explicitly named human vow in Scripture. The Hebrew neder creates a binding self-obligation; vows become a major category in biblical law (Num 30; Deut 23:21–23) and rabbinic ethics. The conditional structure (“If God will be with me… then Yahweh will be my God”) has occasioned debate: is Jacob bargaining? Most commentators read the conditional as not bargaining but recognition — Jacob accepts the divine promise just made (28:13–15) and vows responsive worship. The pattern of vow-as-response-to-revelation recurs throughout the Hebrew Bible.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s tithe. Jacob’s pledge of a tenth is the second tithe-instance in Scripture, after Abraham’s tithe to Melchizedek (14:20). The two patriarchal tithes establish tithing as proto-Israelite practice, prior to the Levitical legal codification (Lev 27:30; Num 18:21–32). Neither Abraham’s nor Jacob’s tithe specifies recipient or use — they are pure responsive offerings. The Mosaic system later distributes tithes (to Levites, festivals, the poor) but the patriarchal model emphasizes the gesture’s responsive character: tithing as acknowledgment that all comes from God.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s tears. Jacob weeps upon meeting Rachel — the verse pairs his kiss with weeping. Rabbinic tradition (Bereshit Rabbah 70:12) gives multiple readings: he wept because he came empty-handed (unlike Eliezer who came laden with gifts for Rebekah, ch 24); because he foresaw she would not be buried with him (35:19, Rachel buried at Bethlehem rather than Machpelah); or simply from emotional intensity. The detail humanizes Jacob — the trickster of the previous chapters becomes the lover overcome at sight of his beloved. The narrative shifts register from family politics to romance.

↩ ◇ Note. Bone and flesh. Laban’s recognition of Jacob as “bone and flesh” uses the same idiom Adam used of Eve (2:23) and David’s tribes use of the king (2 Sam 5:1). The phrase identifies kinship — not metaphor but legal-genealogical claim. Laban’s invocation seems hospitable but the next chapters reveal manipulation: he accepts Jacob’s labor for fourteen years on the basis of this kinship without paying wages until forced. The phrase’s reuse here, in light of its Edenic origin, ironizes covenant kinship — bone-and-flesh language can mask exploitation as much as honor solidarity.

↩ ◇ Note. Bride-price by labor. Jacob’s seven-year labor as bride-price (mohar) in lieu of payment is a documented ANE practice — the Code of Hammurabi (§§159–161) discusses similar arrangements when a groom cannot pay the standard price. Jacob, fleeing his brother’s anger and arriving with no possessions, has only labor to offer. The seven-year period (later doubled to fourteen for both wives) becomes a paradigm of the long-suffering lover — Hosea later uses bride-price imagery for divine love (Hos 3:2). The pattern frames marriage as costly covenant, not merely contract.

↩ ◇ Note. Time transformed by love. The verse’s compression — seven years pass like a few days — is among the Bible’s most famous expressions of how love transforms temporal experience. The narrative voice rarely intrudes for romantic comment; here it does. The phenomenology of love-distorted time has shaped Christian mystical and philosophical reflection (Augustine, Confessions XI; the Song of Songs). The verse will be ironized by what follows — the night Jacob discovers Leah, time will reverse and the seven-year preparation will produce wrong outcome through Laban’s deception.

↩ ◇ Note. Reuben’s name. Reuben’s name (Reʾuven, רְאוּבֵן) word-plays on “see, a son” (reʾu ben) and also on Yahweh’s “seeing” (raʾah) Leah’s affliction. Each of Leah’s sons receives a name connected to her marital pain — the names trace her hope of winning Jacob’s love. Reuben (“see, a son”), Simeon (“heard”), Levi (“joined”), Judah (“I will praise”). The naming patterns reveal the underlying matriarchal subjectivity often eclipsed in patriarchal narrative — the women name the children, encoding their experience into Israel’s tribal identities.

↩ ◇ Note. “Am I in God’s place?” Jacob’s retort sharply distinguishes divine and human prerogatives — only God opens the womb (Hebrew idiom peter rechem). The phrase becomes a paradigm for the limit of human responsibility: certain blessings are not in human power to give. The same logic appears at Joseph’s response to his brothers (50:19, “Am I in the place of God?”), creating a verbal frame for the Jacob narrative — both bookended by acknowledgments of divine prerogative. Jacob’s anger here, however, is theologically ambiguous: he refuses the role of God but treats his wife harshly.

↩ ◇ Note. “On my knees” — adoption ritual. The phrase “bear upon my knees” (ʿal birkay) is an ANE adoption gesture — the legal mother receives the child onto her lap or knees as an act of formal adoption. The Code of Hammurabi (§170) attests to similar adoption ceremonies. Bilhah’s children become Rachel’s by this ritual; the same pattern enables Leah’s adoption of Zilpah’s sons (30:9–13). The four “maidservant-tribes” (Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher) are thus legally Rachel’s and Leah’s despite biological maternity — the inheritance system supports adoptive kinship as fully equivalent.

↩ ◇ Note. Dan = he judged. Rachel names the first surrogate-son Dan (Dan, דָּן, from the verb din, “to judge”). She means Dan’s birth is divine judicial vindication of her plea. The verb din appears most commonly in legal contexts; Rachel’s appeal frames her relation to God as forensic — she has been heard in cosmic court. The Tribe of Dan later becomes the legendary tribe of judges (Samson, Judges 13–16), and Genesis 49:16 pronounces “Dan shall judge his people.” The pun encoded in his name’s etymology persists into Israel’s tribal identity.

↩ ◇ Note. God remembered Rachel. The verb zakhar (“remember”) in biblical Hebrew rarely denotes mere recall — it implies action grounded in covenant relationship. God “remembered” Noah at the flood’s turning point (8:1), Abraham at Sodom (19:29), and now Rachel. The pattern establishes “remembrance” as the trigger of divine action. Rachel’s barrenness is finally answered — Joseph’s birth is the climax of her long-deferred hope. The phrase reappears in Luke 1:54 (Mary’s Magnificat) where God “has remembered his mercy,” and in 1:72 (Zechariah’s Benedictus) where God “remembers his holy covenant.”

↩ ◇ Note. Rachel’s cry. Rachel’s despair phrases her barrenness in life-and-death terms. The cry is theologically and psychologically extreme: childlessness as social death in ancient society (a woman’s worth often measured by progeny), and existential anguish more broadly. Hannah’s parallel anguish at 1 Samuel 1 includes weeping but stops short of Rachel’s threat. Rabbinic tradition (b. Bava Batra 17b) notes Rachel ultimately does die in childbirth (35:18), giving her cry tragic foreshadowing. Modern feminist readings have foregrounded the verse as the Bible’s strongest expression of female reproductive desperation.

↩ ◇ Note. Laban’s gods. Laban’s reaction reveals the religious texture of his household: he genuinely believes the teraphim are “my gods” — not merely cultural artifacts. The patriarchal narratives quietly attest to polytheism within Abraham’s own extended family (cf. Joshua 24:2, “your fathers… served other gods”). Jacob’s family is in contact with this older household religion through Rachel and Leah. The Laban incident frames the long process of Israel’s emergence from polytheistic Mesopotamian context — a process Joshua’s farewell speech (Josh 24:14–15) explicitly recalls.

↩ ◇ Note. The Fear of Isaac. The unusual divine epithet Pachad Yitzhak (פַּחַד יִצְחָק, “Fear of Isaac”) appears here and at 31:53. Three readings dominate: (1) “fear” = the One feared/worshiped by Isaac, an objective genitive; (2) “fear” = numinous awe, the Otto tremendum; (3) connected to Akkadian puchru (assembly), the God of Isaac’s clan. Albright’s scholarship developed option 3, identifying the epithet with patriarchal clan-deity religion. The phrase is one of several distinctive patriarchal divine names (Mighty One of Jacob, Shield of Abraham) preserved in oldest poetic strata.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. ʼădônây (אֲדֹנָי). the Lord (used as a proper name of God only).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: CONTRACTS, COVENANT, LABAN, STONES.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MIZPAH or Miz’peh, watch-tower; the look-out. (1.) A place in Gilead, so named by Laban, who overtook Jacob at this spot (Genesis 31:49) on his return to Palestine from Padan-aram. Here Jacob and Laban set up their memorial cairn of stones. It is the same as Ramath-mizpeh (Joshua 13:26). (2.) A town in Gilead, where Jephthah resided, and where he assumed the command of the Israelites in a time of national danger. Here he made his rash vow; and here his daughter submitted to her mysterious fate (Judges 10:17; 11:11, 34). It may be the same as Ramoth-Gilead (Joshua 20:8), but it is more likely that it is identical with the foregoing, the Mizpeh of Genesis 31:23, 25, 48, 49. (3.) Another place in Gilead, at the foot of Mount Hermon, inhabited by Hivites (Joshua 11:3, 8). The name in Hebrew here has the article before it, “the Mizpeh,” “the watch-tower.” The modern village of Metullah, meaning also “the look-out,” probably occupies the site so called. (4.) A town of Moab to which David removed his parents for safety during his persecution by Saul (1 Samuel 22:3). This was probably the citadel known as Kir-Moab, now Kerak. While David resided here he was visited by the prophet Gad, here mentioned for the first time, who was probably sent by Samuel to bid him leave the land of Moab and betake himself to the land of Judah. He accordingly removed to the forest of Hareth (q.v.), on the edge of the mountain chain of Hebron. (5.) A city of Benjamin, “the watch-tower”, where the people were accustomed to meet in great national emergencies (Joshua 18:26; Judges 20:1, 3; 21:1, 5; 1 Samuel 7:5-16). It has been supposed to be the same as Nob (1 Samuel 21:1; 22:9-19). It was some 4 miles north-west of Jerusalem, and was situated on the loftiest hill in the neighbourhood, some 600 feet above the plain of Gibeon. This village has the modern name of Neby Samwil, i.e., the prophet Samuel, from a tradition that Samuel’s tomb is here. (See NOB.) Samuel inaugurated the reformation that characterized his time by convening a great assembly of all Israel at Mizpeh, now the politico-religious centre of the nation. There, in deep humiliation on account of their sins, they renewed their vows and entered again into covenant with the God of their fathers. It was a period of great religious awakening and of revived national life. The Philistines heard of this assembly, and came up against Israel. The Hebrews charged the Philistine host with great fury, and they were totally routed. Samuel commemorated this signal victory by erecting a memorial-stone, which he called “Ebenezer” (q.v.), saying, “Hitherto hath the Lord helped us” (1 Samuel 7:7-12).

↩ ◇ Note. Distinct ancestral deities. Laban swears by “the God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father” — Jacob swears by “the Fear of his father Isaac.” The asymmetric divine identifications are theologically significant: each side invokes its own ancestral god. The “God of their father” may simply be the unnamed god common to both Abraham and Nahor, or distinct deities. The text preserves a memory of clan-religion before strict monotheism — each patriarchal line associated with its own God-relationship, eventually unified under the name Yahweh.

↩ ◇ Note. Mahanaim — two camps. Jacob meets a band of angels and names the place Mahanaim (“two camps”). The doubled name suggests the meeting of heavenly and earthly hosts. The site reappears in 2 Samuel 17:24 as David’s refuge during Absalom’s rebellion. The Mahanaim encounter functions narratively as inclusio with Bethel (28:12, the angel-stairway) — angels frame Jacob’s exile, marking both the journey out and the journey home. The narrative treats angelic encounter as a regular feature of patriarchal experience rather than rare miracle.

↩ ◇ Note. Wrestling at the Jabbok. The Jabbok wrestling is one of the most theologically dense scenes in Genesis. The wrestler’s identity is unclear — “a man” (32:24), then “God” (32:30), then identified by Hosea 12:4 as “the angel.” The ambiguity is deliberate: the night encounter resists resolution. Karl Barth read it as the paradigm of all encounter with God — God comes as adversary before becoming blesser. The dislocation of Jacob’s hip becomes a permanent mark — covenant blessing cannot be received without wounding. Jewish kosher law (Gen 32:32) traces a dietary practice to this verse.

↩ ◇ Note. The name Israel. The new name Yisraʾel (יִשְׂרָאֵל) is etymologized from sarah (“to strive, contend”) plus El (“God”) — “he strives with God.” The renaming pattern (Abram→Abraham, Jacob→Israel) marks covenant-vocational transitions. Both names persist — Jacob continues to be called Jacob throughout the rest of Genesis. The duality (Jacob/Israel) becomes the literary identity of the people: still the trickster, still the contender, but also the chosen. Hosea 12:3–4 reuses the renaming as a moral exemplar of seeking God’s face.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: CURIOSITY, GOD, ISRAEL, JESUS, THE CHRIST, PRAYER.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Boldness, Holy, Christ is God, Communion of the Lord’s Supper, Prayer, Answers To.

↩ ◇ Note. Peniel. Jacob names the place Peniel (פְּנִיאֵל, “face of God”) — claiming to have seen God face-to-face and survived. The claim is theologically remarkable, since seeing God’s face is later said to be deadly (Ex 33:20, “no man shall see me and live”). Different traditions resolve the tension differently: Targum Onkelos paraphrases as “I have seen the angel of the Lord”; Augustine and patristic tradition read the wrestler as Christological pre-incarnation. The verse establishes a category of theophanic encounter — incomplete vision but survivable — that recurs at Exodus 24:10–11 and Isaiah 6.

↩ ◇ Note. Esau’s face as God’s face. Jacob’s startling claim — “I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God” — pairs directly with Peniel (32:30, “I have seen God face to face”). The doubled use of the face-of-God motif theologizes the human encounter: Jacob’s wrestling with God prepared him to see God in his brother’s face. Levinas’s philosophical theology of “the face of the other” draws explicitly on this Genesis tradition — the human face is the locus of ethical encounter and irreducibly other. The reconciliation with Esau is theologically continuous with the wrestling at Jabbok.

↩ ◇ Note. Pace of the cattle. Jacob’s gentle excuse — proceeding at the pace of cattle and children — is sometimes read as continuing deception (Jacob never actually goes to Seir to meet Esau; he settles in Succoth, 33:17). Other readings see Jacob as genuinely thoughtful caretaker, refusing to push his vulnerable household at warrior-pace. The phrase has become proverbial for slow caretaking leadership — adopted by Pope Gregory the Great in his Pastoral Rule on the bishop as shepherd (Bk II.5). Whether sincere or evasive, the verse models patient leadership.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob arrives in peace. The Hebrew shalem here is grammatically ambiguous — it can mean “in peace” (as a state) or “Salem” (a place name, possibly Salim near Shechem). The “in peace” reading frames the verse as the climax of Jacob’s exile journey: he left in fear (28:10) and returns in peace. The verse’s sequel (the Dinah catastrophe of ch 34) immediately complicates the “peace” — Jacob’s peace is fragile and short-lived. The narrative structure (peace immediately followed by violation) becomes paradigmatic in the Hebrew Bible: settled peace is never the end of the story.

↩ ◇ Note. Dinah. Dinah’s appearance is both abrupt and incomplete — she is the only named daughter of Jacob (although “daughters” are mentioned at 37:35), and the chapter that bears her involvement is told entirely through male voices. She speaks no word in the chapter that bears her assault. Modern feminist criticism (Esther Fuchs, Phyllis Trible) reads the chapter’s silencing as both narrative fact and moral indictment. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan’s expansive paraphrase fills in Dinah’s voice; modern fictional retellings (Anita Diamant’s The Red Tent) do similarly. The text’s silence has provoked centuries of readerly response.

↩ ◇ Note. Folly in Israel. The phrase nevalah be-Yisraʾel (נְבָלָה בְיִשְׂרָאֵל, “folly in Israel”) is a technical Hebrew term for a serious moral and social outrage — used of the Levite’s concubine (Judg 19:23–24), Achan’s transgression (Josh 7:15), Tamar’s rape (2 Sam 13:12). The word nevalah denotes far more than “folly” — it is a category-violation, an act that disrupts communal order. The phrase here serves as the Bible’s first appearance of this technical term — and remarkably, it predates the formation of Israel as a people, indicating the editorial perspective is later than the events narrated.

↩ ◇ Note. Deceit answers violation. The brothers’ deceitful response — agreeing to circumcision in apparent acceptance — uses the covenant sign as a weapon. The chapter’s moral structure is layered: Shechem’s violation, the brothers’ deception of the Shechemites, the city’s mass murder. The narrator describes but does not explicitly judge — leaving the moral evaluation to Jacob’s later denunciation (49:5–7, “Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords”). Critics have read the chapter as theologically pessimistic: covenant practices can be weaponized, and the response to evil produces further evil.

↩ ◇ Note. The third-day attack. The post-circumcision third day was when wound infection peaked — the Shechemite men were physically incapacitated, unable to defend themselves. The detail underscores the calculated nature of Simeon and Levi’s attack. The “third day” motif resonates with later biblical usage (Exodus 19:11, the third-day theophany at Sinai; Hosea 6:2, “after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up”) — but inverted here as a day of violence rather than restoration. The pattern of using sacred timing for unholy purpose anticipates prophetic critique of weaponized religion.

↩ ◇ Note. Putting away foreign gods. Jacob commands his household to dispose of foreign gods — the first explicit Israelite gesture of religious purification. The elohei nekhar (“foreign gods”) likely include Rachel’s stolen teraphim (31:19) and other household deities. The command is paired with ritual ablution (“purify yourselves”) and changing of garments — the elements that later structure pilgrimage to the temple. The pattern recurs at Joshua 24:14–15 (“put away the gods that your fathers served”) and 1 Samuel 7:3 (Samuel’s call). Jacob’s command anticipates the Mosaic prohibitions while predating them.

↩ ◇ Note. El-Bethel revisited. Jacob’s return to Bethel completes the inclusio begun at 28:12 — he left there with a vision of the heavenly stairway, returns with his household and ritually consecrates the site. The new altar-name El-Bethel (“God of the house of God”) joins divine name and place name, theologizing the geography. The pattern of return-to-altar-of-departure becomes a paradigm for biblical pilgrimage — the holy place is constituted not by intrinsic sacredness but by relationship of memory and revelation.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Nephesh (נֶפֶשׁ). properly, a breathing creature, i.e. animal of (abstractly) vitality; used very widely in a literal, accommodated or figurative sense (bodily or mental).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died,) that she called his name Ben-oni: but his father called him Benjamin'. Ephrem reads the double-naming as the dialectic of grief-and-hope: the mother dying names her son Son-of-my-sorrow; the father renames him Son-of-the-right-hand (i.e., Son-of-strength / favoured-son). Tewahedo pastoral theology preserves this pattern: the church speaks both griefs honestly AND reframes them into hope, never denying the first.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BENJAMIN son of my right hand. (1.) The younger son of Jacob by Rachel (Genesis 35:18). His birth took place at Ephrath, on the road between Bethel and Bethlehem, at a short distance from the latter place. His mother died in giving him birth, and with her last breath named him Ben-oni, son of my pain, a name which was changed by his father into Benjamin. His posterity are called Benjamites (Genesis 49:27; Deuteronomy 33:12; Joshua 18:21). The tribe of Benjamin at the Exodus was the smallest but one (Numbers 1:36, 37; Psalm 68:27). During the march its place was along with Manasseh and Ephraim on the west of the tabernacle. At the entrance into Canaan it counted 45,600 warriors. It has been inferred by some from the words of Jacob (Genesis 49:27) that the figure of a wolf was on the tribal standard. This tribe is mentioned in Romans 11:1; Phil. 3:5. The inheritance of this tribe lay immediately to the south of that of Ephraim, and was about 26 miles in length and 12 in breadth. Its eastern boundary was the Jordan. Dan intervened between it and the Philistines. Its chief towns are named in Joshua 18:21-28. The history of the tribe contains a sad record of a desolating civil war in which they were engaged with the other eleven tribes. By it they were almost exterminated (Judges 20:20, 21; 21:10). (See GIBEAH.) The first king of the Jews was Saul, a Benjamite. A close alliance was formed between this tribe and that of Judah in the time of David (2 Samuel 19:16, 17), which continued after his death (1 Kings 11:13; 12:20). After the Exile these two tribes formed the great body of the Jewish nation (Ezra 1:5; 10:9). The tribe of Benjamin was famous for its archers (1 Samuel 20:20, 36; 2 Samuel 1:22; 1 Chronicles 8:40; 12:2) and slingers (Judge. 20:6). The gate of Benjamin, on the north side of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 37:13; 38:7; Zechariah 14:10), was so called because it led in the direction of the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. It is called by Jeremiah (20:2) “the high gate of Benjamin;” also “the gate of the children of the people” (17:19). (Comp. 2 Kings 14:13.)

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Benjamin, Tribe Of, Children.

↩ ◇ Note. Rachel’s tomb. Rachel is the only matriarch buried outside Machpelah — buried instead on the road to Bethlehem (35:19). Jeremiah 31:15 invokes her: “a voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children.” Matthew 2:18 cites this verse at the slaughter of the innocents — Rachel’s geographic burial-place becomes the eschatological figure of all maternal grief. The tomb (now in modern Bethlehem) remains a major Jewish pilgrimage site. The geography is theological: Rachel buried at the gate of Bethlehem positions her as eternal weeper for the line that will produce David and Christ.

'And it came to pass... that Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine: and Israel heard it'. Ephrem reads Reuben's sin as the COVENANT-RUPTURE moment that cost him the firstborn's inheritance (cf. Gen 49:3-4, 1 Chr 5:1) — Reuben's primogeniture passes to Joseph by way of the double-portion-to-his-two-sons. Tewahedo monastic-discipline tradition cites Reuben's example: a single major moral failure can cost ecclesiastical office, even when individual salvation remains.

↩ ◇ Note. Isaac’s death. Isaac dies at 180, the longest-lived of the patriarchs (Abraham 175, Jacob 147). The verse pairs his death with burial by both sons — Esau and Jacob together, in apparent reconciliation. The detail echoes 25:9 (Isaac and Ishmael burying Abraham together). Family conflicts that dominate the patriarchal narratives are framed by funerary cooperation — death produces a brief solidarity that life could not sustain. Isaac’s narrative ends quietly; the chapter following turns immediately to the line of Esau (ch 36) before resuming the line of Jacob (ch 37).

↩ ◇ Note. Esau’s toledot. Genesis 36 is one of two genealogical chapters devoted to Esau (the other is the king-list at 36:31–43), reflecting the editorial principle that disinherited or non-chosen lines receive their genealogy before the chosen line continues. The pattern recurs: Cain’s line (4:17–22) before Seth’s; Ishmael (25:12–18) before Isaac; Esau (here) before Jacob (37:2). The structural choice has theological weight — even non-chosen lines are recorded with care, suggesting that election is selective rather than annihilating, and that the rejected branch’s history matters.

↩ ◇ Note. Geographic separation. Esau’s withdrawal from the land — too crowded for both — formally cedes Canaan to Jacob’s line. The phrasing echoes Abraham and Lot’s earlier separation (13:9–11) where Lot chose the better-watered Jordan plain. Both scenes establish boundaries by departure rather than treaty. Esau’s settling in Seir (the future Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea) creates the geographic stage for the long Israelite-Edomite enmity that culminates in the prophetic oracles against Edom (Obadiah; Mal 1:2–4).

↩ ◇ Note. Amalek. Amalek, here noted as the son of Eliphaz (Esau’s son) by his concubine Timna, becomes the eponym of Israel’s bitterest perpetual enemy. Exodus 17:8–16 describes Amalek’s unprovoked attack on Israel in the wilderness; Deuteronomy 25:17–19 commands Israel to “blot out the remembrance of Amalek”; 1 Samuel 15 records Saul’s failed extermination, costing him the kingdom; Esther’s villain Haman is identified as Agagite (Amalekite descendant). The genealogical note here makes Amalek’s enmity primordial — already encoded in the family tree before any historical encounter.

↩ ◇ Note. Anah and the hot springs. The detail of Anah finding hot springs (Hebrew yemim, יֵמִם — a hapax legomenon, otherwise unattested) is unusually specific within a genealogical chapter. The word’s meaning is debated — Vulgate renders “hot springs,” others suggest “mules” (folk etymology) or “water sources.” The detail anchors the genealogy in concrete geographic memory: the dry Edomite hill-country has hot springs, and a particular ancestor is remembered as their discoverer. The chapter’s preservation of such mundane detail underscores its function as authentic genealogical archive.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SAUL asked for. (1.) A king of Edom (Genesis 36:37, 38); called Shaul in 1 Chronicles 1:48. (2.) The son of Kish (probably his only son, and a child of prayer, “asked for”), of the tribe of Benjamin, the first king of the Jewish nation. The singular providential circumstances connected with his election as king are recorded in 1 Samuel 8-10. His father’s she-asses had strayed, and Saul was sent with a servant to seek for them. Leaving his home at Gibeah (10:5, “the hill of God,” A.V.; lit., as in R.V. marg., “Gibeah of God”), Saul and his servant went toward the north-west over Mount Ephraim, and then turning north-east they came to “the land of Shalisha,” and thence eastward to the land of Shalim, and at length came to the district of Zuph, near Samuel’s home at Ramah (9:5-10). At this point Saul proposed to return from the three days’ fruitless search, but his servant suggested that they should first consult the “seer.” Hearing that he was about to offer sacrifice, the two hastened into Ramah, and “behold, Samuel came out against them,” on his way to the “bamah”, i.e., the “height”, where sacrifice was to be offered; and in answer to Saul’s question, “Tell me, I pray thee, where the seer’s house is,” Samuel made himself known to him. Samuel had been divinely prepared for his coming (9:15-17), and received Saul as his guest. He took him with him to the sacrifice, and then after the feast “communed with Saul upon the top of the house” of all that was in his heart. On the morrow Samuel “took a vial of oil and poured it on his head,” and anointed Saul as king over Israel (9:25-10:8), giving him three signs in confirmation of his call to be king. When Saul reached his home in Gibeah the last of these signs was fulfilled, and the Sprit of God came upon him, and “he was turned into another man.” The simple countryman was transformed into the king of Israel, a remarkable change suddenly took place in his whole demeanour, and the people said in their astonishment, as they looked on the stalwart son of Kish, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”, a saying which passed into a “proverb.” (Comp. 19:24.) The intercourse between Saul and Samuel was as yet unknown to the people. The “anointing” had been in secret. But now the time had come when the transaction must be confirmed by the nation. Samuel accordingly summoned the people to a solemn assembly “before the Lord” at Mizpeh. Here the lot was drawn (10:17-27), and it fell upon Saul, and when he was presented before them, the stateliest man in all Israel, the air was rent for the first time in Israel by the loud cry, “God save the king!” He now returned to his home in Gibeah, attended by a kind of bodyguard, “a band of men whose hearts God had touched.” On reaching his home he dismissed them, and resumed the quiet toils of his former life. Soon after this, on hearing of the conduct of Nahash the Ammonite at Jabeshgilead (q.v.), an army out of all the tribes of Israel rallied at his summons to the trysting-place at Bezek, and he led them forth a great army to battle, gaining a complete victory over the Ammonite invaders at Jabesh (11:1-11). Amid the universal joy occasioned by this victory he was now fully recognized as the king of Israel. At the invitation of Samuel “all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the Lord in Gilgal.” Samuel now officially anointed him as king (11:15). Although Samuel never ceased to be a judge in Israel, yet now his work in that capacity practically came to an end. Saul now undertook the great and difficult enterprise of freeing the land from its hereditary enemies the Philistines, and for this end he gathered together an army of 3,000 men (1 Samuel 13:1, 2). The Philistines were encamped at Geba. Saul, with 2,000 men, occupied Michmash and Mount Bethel; while his son Jonathan, with 1,000 men, occupied Gibeah, to the south of Geba, and seemingly without any direction from his father “smote” the Philistines in Geba. Thus roused, the Philistines, who gathered an army of 30,000 chariots and 6,000 horsemen, and “people as the sand which is on the sea-shore in multitude,” encamped in Michmash, which Saul had evacuated for Gilgal. Saul now tarried for seven days in Gilgal before making any movement, as Samuel had appointed (10:8); but becoming impatient on the seventh day, as it was drawing to a close, when he had made an end of offering the burnt offering, Samuel appeared and warned him of the fatal consequences of his act of disobedience, for he had not waited long enough (13:13, 14). When Saul, after Samuel’s departure, went out from Gilgal with his 600 men, his followers having decreased to that number (13:15), against the Philistines at Michmash (q.v.), he had his head-quarters under a pomegrante tree at Migron, over against Michmash, the Wady esSuweinit alone intervening. Here at Gibeah-Geba Saul and his army rested, uncertain what to do. Jonathan became impatient, and with his armour-bearer planned an assault against the Philistines, unknown to Saul and the army (14:1-15). Jonathan and his armour-bearer went down into the wady, and on their hands and knees climbed to the top of the narrow rocky ridge called Bozez, where was the outpost of the Philistine army. They surprised and then slew twenty of the Philistines, and immediately the whole host of the Philistines was thrown into disorder and fled in great terror. “It was a very great trembling;” a supernatural panic seized the host. Saul and his 600 men, a band which speedily increased to 10,000, perceiving the confusion, pursued the army of the Philistines, and the tide of battle rolled on as far as to Bethaven, halfway between Michmash and Bethel. The Philistines were totally routed. “So the Lord saved Israel that day.” While pursuing the Philistines, Saul rashly adjured the people, saying, “Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening.” But though faint and weary, the Israelites “smote the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon” (a distance of from 15 to 20 miles). Jonathan had, while passing through the wood in pursuit of the Philistines, tasted a little of the honeycomb which was abundant there (14:27). This was afterwards discovered by Saul (ver. 42), and he threatened to put his son to death. The people, however, interposed, saying, “There shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground.” He whom God had so signally owned, who had “wrought this great salvation in Israel,” must not die. “Then Saul went up from following the Philistines: and the Philistines went to their own place” (1 Samuel 14:24-46); and thus the campaign against the Philistines came to an end. This was Saul’s second great military success. Saul’s reign, however, continued to be one of almost constant war against his enemies round about (14:47, 48), in all of which he proved victorious. The war against the Amalekites is the only one which is recorded at length (1 Samuel 15). These oldest and hereditary (Exodus 17:8; Numbers 14:43-45) enemies of Israel occupied the territory to the south and south-west of Palestine. Samuel summoned Saul to execute the “ban” which God had pronounced (Deuteronomy 25:17-19) on this cruel and relentless foe of Israel. The cup of their iniquity was now full. This command was “the test of his moral qualification for being king.” Saul proceeded to execute the divine command; and gathering the people together, marched from Telaim (1 Samuel 15:4) against the Amalekites, whom he smote “from Havilah until thou comest to Shur,” utterly destroying “all the people with the edge of the sword”, i.e., all that fell into his hands. He was, however, guilty of rebellion and disobedience in sparing Agag their king, and in conniving at his soldiers’ sparing the best of the sheep and cattle; and Samuel, following Saul to Gilgal, in the Jordan valley, said unto him, “Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he also hath rejected thee from being king” (15:23). The kingdom was rent from Saul and was given to another, even to David, whom the Lord chose to be Saul’s successor, and whom Samuel anointed (16:1-13). From that day “the spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” He and Samuel parted only to meet once again at one of the schools of the prophets. David was now sent for as a “cunning player on an harp” (1 Samuel 16:16, 18), to play before Saul when the evil spirit troubled him, and thus was introduced to the court of Saul. He became a great favourite with the king. At length David returned to his father’s house and to his wonted avocation as a shepherd for perhaps some three years. The Philistines once more invaded the land, and gathered their army between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim, on the southern slope of the valley of Elah. Saul and the men of Israel went forth to meet them, and encamped on the northern slope of the same valley which lay between the two armies. It was here that David slew Goliath of Gath, the champion of the Philistines (17:4-54), an exploit which led to the flight and utter defeat of the Philistine army. Saul now took David permanently into his service (18:2); but he became jealous of him (ver. 9), and on many occasions showed his enmity toward him (ver. 10, 11), his enmity ripening into a purpose of murder which at different times he tried in vain to carry out. After some time the Philistines “gathered themselves together” in the plain of Esdraelon, and pitched their camp at Shunem, on the slope of Little Hermon; and Saul “gathered all Israel together,” and “pitched in Gilboa” (1 Samuel 28:3-14). Being unable to discover the mind of the Lord, Saul, accompanied by two of his retinue, betook himself to the “witch of Endor,” some 7 or 8 miles distant. Here he was overwhelmed by the startling communication that was mysteriously made to him by Samuel (ver. 16-19), who appeared to him. “He fell straightway all along on the earth, and was sore afraid, because of the words of Samuel” (ver. 20). The Philistine host “fought against Israel: and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines, and fell down slain in Mount Gilboa” (31:1). In his despair at the disaster that had befallen his army, Saul “took a sword and fell upon it.” And the Philistines on the morrow “found Saul and his three sons fallen in Mount Gilboa.” Having cut off his head, they sent it with his weapons to Philistia, and hung up the skull in the temple of Dagon at Ashdod. They suspended his headless body, with that of Jonathan, from the walls of Bethshan. The men of Jabesh-gilead afterwards removed the bodies from this position; and having burnt the flesh, they buried the bodies under a tree at Jabesh. The remains were, however, afterwards removed to the family sepulchre at Zelah (2 Samuel 21:13, 14). (See DAVID.) (3.) “Who is also called Paul” (q.v.), the circumcision name of the apostle, given to him, perhaps, in memory of King Saul (Acts 7:58; 8:1; 9:1).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Edomites, The.

↩ ◇ Note. Esau as Edom’s father. The chapter’s closing phrase definitively identifies Esau-as-people: not just the patriarch’s individual fate but the founding ancestor of an entire nation. The double identification (Esau / Edom) frames the chapter — opening at 36:1 with “Esau, that is, Edom” and closing here. The literary inclusio reinforces that the chapter’s purpose is national-genealogical, locating the Edomites within the Abrahamic family while distinguishing them from Israel. The Edomites later become the most consistent prophetic targets among Israel’s neighbors precisely because of this kinship.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s evil report. The Hebrew dibbah raʿah (דִּבָּה רָעָה, “evil report, slander”) is morally ambiguous in this verse. Was Joseph reporting his brothers’ actual misconduct (which would be morally licit) or maliciously slandering them? The text leaves it ambiguous, but the chapter’s psychology suggests the brothers experienced his reports as betrayal. The same vocabulary (dibbah) is used of the spies’ false report (Num 14:36) and prophetic critique. The verse opens the Joseph cycle by establishing fraternal tension as a moral-psychological reality, not merely behavioral conflict.

↩ ◇ Note. The sheaves dream. The first of Joseph’s two prophetic dreams uses agricultural imagery — sheaves bowing — that fits a settled-agriculture milieu, not yet Joseph’s eventual Egyptian context. The dream’s prediction is fulfilled at Genesis 42:6 (the brothers bow before the Egyptian governor). The dream-as-prophecy structure becomes paradigmatic for biblical prophetic dreams: not ambiguous but disclosive of future divine plan. Joseph’s two dreams (sheaves, then sun-moon-stars) escalate in cosmic scope — the same pattern of dream-pair structures Pharaoh’s dreams (cows, then grain) at Genesis 41.

↩ ◇ Note. Sun, moon, and stars. Joseph’s second dream uses cosmic imagery — celestial bodies bowing. Father Jacob immediately interprets sun and moon as himself and Rachel, eleven stars as the eleven brothers. The motif’s literary afterlife is rich: Revelation 12:1 reuses the imagery (“a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars”) — typically read as referring to Israel-as-Mary. The eleven-stars-plus-Joseph make twelve, the tribal number. The dream encodes Joseph’s eventual ruling status while paradoxically fueling the brothers’ hatred that brings about its fulfillment.

↩ ◇ Note. The empty pit. The detail “no water in it” signals a dry cistern — depth without drowning, suitable for imprisonment but not for execution. The pit (bor) functions as proto-grave imagery throughout the Hebrew Bible — Joseph’s pit foreshadows Jeremiah’s cistern (Jer 38:6), the “pit” of Sheol (Ps 30:3), and ultimately the tomb. Christian typology has read Joseph’s descent into and emergence from the pit as type of Christ’s death and resurrection. The chapter’s literary structure — descent into pit, sale into Egypt, eventual rise to power — establishes Joseph as paradigmatic suffering-then-glorified figure.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And they... sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver'. Ephrem reads the twenty-pieces-of-silver sale as the OT type of Christ's thirty-pieces-of-silver betrayal: same pattern (the righteous one sold by his own kin for silver-pieces), with the price escalating in the antitype. Tewahedo Holy-Week liturgy explicitly draws the Joseph-typology in the Wednesday-of-Holy-Week readings: Joseph sold prefigures Christ betrayed.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MIDIANITE an Arabian tribe descended from Midian. They inhabited principally the desert north of the peninsula of Arabia. The peninsula of Sinai was the pasture-ground for their flocks. They were virtually the rulers of Arabia, being the dominant tribe. Like all Arabians, they were a nomad people. They early engaged in commercial pursuits. It was to one of their caravans that Joseph was sold (Genesis 37:28, 36). The next notice of them is in connection with Moses’ flight from Egypt (Exodus 2:15-21). Here in Midian Moses became the servant and afterwards the son-in-law of Reuel or Jethro, the priest. After the Exodus, the Midianites were friendly to the Israelites so long as they traversed only their outlying pasture-ground on the west of the Arabah; but when, having passed the southern end of Edom, they entered into the land of Midian proper, they joined with Balak, the king of Moab, in a conspiracy against them (Numbers 22:4-7). Balaam, who had been sent for to curse Israel, having utterly failed to do so, was dismissed by the king of Moab; nevertheless he still tarried among the Midianites, and induced them to enter into correspondence with the Israelites, so as to bring them into association with them in the licentious orgies connected with the worship of Baal-Peor. This crafty counsel prevailed. The Israelites took part in the heathen festival, and so brought upon themselves a curse indeed. Their apostasy brought upon them a severe punishment. A plague broke out amongst them, and more than twenty-four thousand of the people perished (Numbers 25:9). But the Midianites were not to be left unpunished. A terrible vengeance was denounced against them. A thousand warriors from each tribe, under the leadership of Phinehas, went forth against them. The Midianites were utterly routed. Their cities were consumed by fire, five of their kings were put to death, and the whole nation was destroyed (Joshua 13:21, 22). Balaam also perished by the sword, receiving the “wages of his unrighteousness” (Numbers 31:8; 2 Peter 2:15). The whole of the country on the east of Jordan, now conquered by the Israelites (see SIHON; OG), was divided between the two tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh. Some two hundred and fifty years after this the Midianites had regained their ancient power, and in confederation with the Amalekites and the “children of the east” they made war against their old enemies the Israelites, whom for seven years they oppressed and held in subjection. They were at length assailed by Gideon in that ever-memorable battle in the great plain of Esdraelon, and utterly destroyed (Judges 6:1-ch. 7). Frequent allusions are afterwards made to this great victory (Psalm 83:10, 12; Isaiah 9:4; 10:6). They now wholly pass away from the page of history both sacred and profane.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Dead, The, Dead, The, Represented by the.

↩ ◇ Note. Sheol — the first occurrence. Jacob’s lament contains the first occurrence of Sheʾol (שְׁאוֹל) in the Bible — the underworld realm of the dead. Sheol is morally undifferentiated in the early Hebrew Bible — both righteous and wicked descend there. The development from Sheol into the bipartite afterlife (Paradise + Gehenna) emerges only later, especially in Second Temple Judaism. Jacob’s invocation of Sheol-reunion (“I will go down to my son”) hints at conceptions of postmortem family reunion that exceed the technical theology of Sheol — a tension between official doctrine and lived hope that recurs throughout the Bible.

↩ ◇ Note. Judah’s narrative interruption. Genesis 38 is famously inserted between Joseph’s sale (ch 37) and his arrival in Egypt (ch 39), interrupting the Joseph narrative just at its dramatic high point. Various interpreters propose different rationales: showing what was happening on the home front during Joseph’s exile; contrasting Judah’s moral failure with Joseph’s faithfulness in Egypt; establishing Judah’s tribal genealogy (which is the messianic line, not Joseph’s). The chapter’s apparent narrative “digression” is theologically central — Perez, the son born to Tamar and Judah, is direct ancestor of David and ultimately of Jesus (Matt 1:3).

↩ ◇ Note. Onan’s act. The verse becomes the source for the term “onanism,” later used (especially in Catholic moral theology) to denote masturbation or non-procreative sexual acts. The original biblical issue, however, is specifically refusal to fulfill the levirate duty (raising offspring for a deceased brother) — an economic-genealogical refusal rather than the act of seed-spilling per se. The text’s “evil in Yahweh’s sight” (38:10) attaches moral weight to the refusal. Modern Catholic moral theology has continued the prohibition on contraception by analogy; Protestant and Jewish traditions generally read the offense more narrowly as levirate-refusal.

↩ ◇ Note. Tamar’s veil. Tamar’s veiling parallels Rebekah’s (24:65), but here functions as disguise rather than modesty — Tamar uses the veil to be mistaken for a prostitute. The tension between modesty and seduction in the same garment is theologically loaded: covering can be revealing depending on context. The veil’s role in the deception eventually serves justice — Tamar gets the offspring legally owed her by Judah’s family. The narrative’s moral evaluation is supplied at 38:26 (“She is more righteous than I”), making this one of the Bible’s clearest cases of female-initiative justice within patriarchal society.

↩ ◇ Note. Identifying tokens. Tamar requires three identifying tokens — signet (chotam), cord (patil), staff (matteh) — the most specific identification possible. The signet was a personal seal-stamp (typically worn on cord around neck), used for legal authentication. Each item identifies Judah uniquely. The triple-pledge ensures Tamar can prove her claim against any denial — anticipating exactly the courtroom moment at 38:25–26. The detail also reveals Judah as economically secure (signet-owning) but morally careless (handing over his identity for a sexual transaction).

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Tsedeq (צֶדֶק). the right (natural, moral or legal); also (abstractly) equity or (figuratively) prosperity.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SCARLET This dye was obtained by the Egyptians from the shell-fish Carthamus tinctorius; and by the Hebrews from the Coccus ilicis, an insect which infests oak trees, called kermes by the Arabians. This colour was early known (Genesis 38:28). It was one of the colours of the ephod (Exodus 28:6), the girdle (8), and the breastplate (15) of the high priest. It is also mentioned in various other connections (Joshua 2:18; 2 Samuel 1:24; Lamentations 4:5; Nahum 2:3). A scarlet robe was in mockery placed on our Lord (Matthew 27:28; Luke 23:11). “Sins as scarlet” (Isaiah 1:18), i.e., as scarlet robes “glaring and habitual.” Scarlet and crimson were the firmest of dyes, and thus not easily washed out.

↩ ◇ Note. Perez — the breach. Perez’s name (פֶּרֶץ, “breach, breaking through”) etymologizes the unusual birth order — the second twin emerging first. The verb paratz (“to break through”) recurs as theological vocabulary throughout the Hebrew Bible, often connected to divine breakthroughs (cf. Mic 2:13). The naming becomes prophetic: Perez breaks through into firstborn position, his line becomes the Davidic-messianic line (Ruth 4:18–22; Matt 1:3). The “breaking through” motif is central — God’s chosen line breaks through expected birth-order conventions, just as Jacob over Esau, Joseph over Reuben, David over his elder brothers.

↩ ◇ Note. Yahweh with Joseph. The phrase Yahweh ʿim Yosef (“Yahweh was with Joseph”) appears four times in this chapter (39:2, 3, 21, 23), forming the chapter’s theological refrain. The same formula structures the Davidic narratives (1 Sam 18:14, “David was prosperous in all his ways, and Yahweh was with him”) and reaches Christological climax at Matthew 1:23 (“Emmanuel, which means God with us”). Joseph’s Egyptian exile becomes the founding paradigm of divine presence in foreign land — God’s presence is not territory-bound but person-bound. The motif sustains exilic theology and the New Testament’s universalist mission.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s beauty. The unusual narrative attention to Joseph’s physical attractiveness (literally “beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance”) is the same vocabulary used of his mother Rachel (29:17). Joseph inherits Rachel’s beauty — a literary connection that links Joseph to the beloved-but-unacknowledged maternal line. The beauty-detail foreshadows the next scene (Potiphar’s wife’s seduction) and theologizes physical attractiveness as morally complex: it is gift but also danger. The same pattern recurs with David (1 Sam 16:12) and absalom (2 Sam 14:25) — beauty as both blessing and trial.

↩ ◇ Note. The seductive gaze. Potiphar’s wife’s “lifting of her eyes” to Joseph (Hebrew vatissaʾ … ʿeyneha) is the standard biblical idiom for active sexual interest. Tellingly, the text presents her as the active seducer — a reversal of typical ANE narrative where men pursue. The story’s pattern (faithful Joseph resists, woman accuses falsely, Joseph imprisoned) parallels the ancient Egyptian “Tale of Two Brothers” — making this one of the clearest cases of Hebrew Bible adaptation of Egyptian narrative material. The Hebrew narrative theologizes the type by introducing Yahweh as ground of Joseph’s resistance.

↩ ◇ Note. The left garment. Joseph’s flight, leaving his garment behind, is the third time clothing serves as evidence in the Joseph narrative: (1) his bloodied tunic at 37:31–33; (2) here; (3) Pharaoh’s signet-and-robe at 41:42 in his eventual elevation. The pattern of identity-clothing recurs throughout Joseph’s story — clothing as markers of social status that are repeatedly stripped and given. Theologians have read the motif as type of Christ stripped of garments at crucifixion (John 19:23–24) and clothed in white at resurrection. Joseph repeatedly loses clothes only to receive better ones.

↩ ◇ Note. Prison without trial. The narrative passes lightly over what should have been a capital offense — adultery with a master’s wife, in Egyptian law, would have been punished by death. Yet Potiphar imprisons rather than executes. Many commentators (Sarna, Speiser) read this leniency as suggesting Potiphar may have doubted his wife’s account but could not openly challenge her. The detail preserves Joseph’s life for the providential plot. The downward trajectory (sold → enslaved → imprisoned) represents Joseph’s deepest descent before his eventual elevation — modeling the biblical pattern of humiliation-before-exaltation that informs Philippians 2:5–11.

↩ ◇ Note. Paired dreams. The cup-bearer and baker share the same night for distinct dreams — a literary doubling that creates dramatic tension. Each dream awaits interpretation; their interpretations diverge sharply (one to restoration, one to execution). The pattern recurs at chapter 41 with Pharaoh’s paired dreams (cows + grain) — both meaning the same thing, doubled for emphasis (41:32). The Joseph cycle uses dream-pairs as a structural feature: Joseph’s two dreams (37), prisoners’ two dreams (40), Pharaoh’s two dreams (41). Each dream-pair expands in cosmic significance from family to royal household to nation.

↩ ◇ Note. The royal cup. The cup-bearer’s dream centers on Pharaoh’s cup — Egyptian royal court iconography is well-attested archaeologically, with cup-bearers (wbꜣ) holding intimate position near the king. The cup as royal symbol resonates throughout the Hebrew Bible — the cup of blessing (Ps 16:5), the cup of wrath (Isa 51:17), Jesus’s “cup” in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). The cup-bearer’s restoration prefigures Joseph’s later cup-trick with his brothers (Gen 44:2) — Joseph plants his own cup as a structural inversion, the wronged man now becoming the one who manipulates cups.

↩ ◇ Note. Two “lift up your head” idioms. The Hebrew idiom “lift up the head” (nasa rosh) carries opposite meanings in 40:13 (cup-bearer restored) and 40:19 (baker beheaded). The same words generate diametrically opposite outcomes — restoration versus decapitation. The wordplay is deliberate, demonstrating Joseph’s interpretive precision. Numbers 1:2’s military census uses the same idiom for “take a count of the head” — counting and beheading share vocabulary. The rhetorical tension between identical phrases pointing to opposite fates becomes a hallmark of biblical wisdom literature.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BASKET There are five different Hebrew words so rendered in the Authorized Version: (1.) A basket (Hebrews sal, a twig or osier) for holding bread (Genesis 40:16; Exodus 29:3, 23; Leviticus 8:2, 26, 31; Numbers 6:15, 17, 19). Sometimes baskets were made of twigs peeled; their manufacture was a recognized trade among the Hebrews. (2.) That used (Hebrews salsilloth’) in gathering grapes (Jeremiah 6:9). (3.) That in which the first fruits of the harvest were presented, Hebrews tene, (Deuteronomy 26:2, 4). It was also used for household purposes. In form it tapered downwards like that called corbis by the Romans. (4.) A basket (Hebrews kelub) having a lid, resembling a bird-cage. It was made of leaves or rushes. The name is also applied to fruit-baskets (Amos 8:1, 2). (5.) A basket (Hebrews dud) for carrying figs (Jeremiah 24:2), also clay to the brick-yard (R.V., Psalm 81:6), and bulky articles (2 Kings 10:7). This word is also rendered in the Authorized Version “kettle” (1 Samuel 2:14), “caldron” (2 Chronicles 35:13), “seething-pot” (Job 41:20). In the New Testament mention is made of the basket (Gr. kophinos, small “wicker-basket”) for the “fragments” in the miracle recorded Mark 6:43, and in that recorded Matthew 15:37 (Gr. spuris, large “rope-basket”); also of the basket in which Paul escaped (Acts 9:25, Gr. spuris; 2 Corinthians 11: 33, Gr. sargane, “basket of plaited cords”).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BEHEAD a method of taking away life practised among the Egyptians (Genesis 40:17-19). There are instances of this mode of punishment also among the Hebrews (2 Samuel 4:8; 20:21,22; 2 Kings 10:6-8). It is also mentioned in the New Testament (Matthew 14:8-12; Acts 12:2).

↩ ◇ Note. The unburied body. The baker’s fate — body unburied, devoured by birds — was the most severe ANE post-mortem disgrace. Burial was understood as essential for proper afterlife; unburied corpses indicated the deceased’s exclusion from family-gathering. The same fate is pronounced on Jezebel (2 Kings 9:36–37). The motif also resonates with Egyptian beliefs about preservation of the body for afterlife — making the baker’s fate especially horrific in his cultural context. Joseph’s interpretation does not soften the message; he tells the truth even when it means death.
