↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Persons confined in.

↩ ◇ Note. The forgotten Joseph. The chapter ends with bitter irony: Joseph is forgotten by the very man whose life he interpreted. The waiting period — “two full years” (41:1) — is theologically central. Joseph’s elevation comes not at human petition but at divine timing through Pharaoh’s own dreams. The pattern teaches biblical providence: human cooperation may be expected and refused, yet the larger plan unfolds without dependence on human reliability. The motif of being forgotten and later remembered structures Israel’s exilic experience — God remembers when humans forget.

↩ ◇ Note. Two full years. The chapter opens with a temporal marker — Joseph waits two years after the cup-bearer’s release before Pharaoh’s dreams trigger his recall. The pause has been read theologically as pedagogical: Joseph’s elevation comes through Pharaoh’s vision, not human petition. The pattern teaches biblical providence’s timing — God’s plans unfold according to divine kairos rather than human urgency. Two years is also significant chronologically — Joseph entered Egypt at 17 (37:2), interpreted Pharaoh’s dreams at 30 (41:46) — meaning roughly two years in prison after the cup-bearer episode.

↩ ◇ Note. Shaving and changing. Joseph’s preparation for Pharaoh — shaving, changing clothes — reflects Egyptian custom rather than Hebrew (Hebrews maintained beards as standard). Egyptian aristocracy and priesthood were clean-shaven; Joseph’s cultural adaptation marks his transition into Egyptian court status. The shave also indicates a fresh role: he leaves behind the prison identity and begins the courtier identity. The triple clothing-motif (Joseph’s bloody tunic, garment left with Potiphar’s wife, here new garments for Pharaoh) marks his trajectory from family-marked to slave-stripped to court-clothed — eventually culminating in Pharaoh’s signet and fine linen at 41:42.

↩ ◇ Note. The doubled dream. Joseph explicitly interprets the doubling of Pharaoh’s dreams as theological emphasis — when God doubles a dream, the matter is fixed and imminent. The pattern of doubling-as-divine-signal has wider biblical resonance: Pharaoh’s two dreams here, the two confirmations Gideon receives (Judg 6:36–40), Jesus’s Transfiguration witnessed by three disciples (Mark 9:2–10) doubling the cloud-voice motif of Sinai. Joseph’s hermeneutical principle — that dream-form encodes divine intention — establishes biblical dream-interpretation as systematic rather than ad hoc.

↩ ◇ Note. Spirit of God. Pharaoh’s recognition that Joseph has “the spirit of God” (ruach Elohim) is theologically remarkable — a pagan king attributing divine indwelling to a Hebrew slave. The phrase is the same one used at creation (Gen 1:2, the Spirit of God hovering over the waters) and recurs in narratives of charismatic leadership (Bezalel at Ex 31:3; the judges; David at 1 Sam 16:13). Pharaoh’s spiritual recognition makes him another biblical Gentile recipient of insight (alongside Abimelech, the wise men of Babylon, Cyrus). The verse legitimates non-Israelite spiritual perception.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s Egyptian name. Pharaoh renames Joseph Tsafenat-Paneach — variously interpreted as “revealer of secrets,” “the god speaks, he lives,” or other Egyptian etymologies. The renaming completes Joseph’s transformation from Hebrew slave to Egyptian official; he also receives an Egyptian wife (Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On). The dual identity (Joseph + Tsafenat) parallels the Daniel/Belteshazzar pattern in Babylon. The Joseph cycle thus models faithful service in foreign court while retaining covenant identity — a model that becomes especially relevant for Diaspora Jewish self-understanding under Persian, Greek, and Roman rule.

↩ ◇ Note. The brothers bow. The brothers’ prostration before Joseph fulfills his sheaves-dream of 37:7 — the brothers bowing down to him. Joseph immediately recognizes the fulfillment (42:9, “Joseph remembered the dreams”). The inclusio between dreams and fulfillment is one of the Hebrew Bible’s most extended dream-prophecy structures, separated by 20+ years of narrative. The pattern teaches biblical providence: dreams that seem absurd at the time of receipt are confirmed by their improbable fulfillment. The brothers do not yet know they fulfill the dream — making the moment heavily ironic in narrative terms.

↩ ◇ Note. The twelve. The brothers identify themselves as twelve (counting Joseph as “no more”). The number twelve becomes Israel’s tribal designation — and the brothers’ self-identification here, even with one missing, asserts the integrity of the tribal whole. The “twelve” pattern recurs throughout biblical history: twelve tribes, twelve apostles, twelve foundations of the eschatological Jerusalem (Rev 21:14). The brothers’ inclusion of Joseph in their count (even calling him deceased) ironically maintains tribal integrity at the moment of standing before him. The narrative quietly encodes the tribal future even at the height of family fracture.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s tears. Joseph’s secret weeping is one of three tears-scenes in the reunion narrative (here; 43:30; 45:2). Each escalates: hidden weeping, retreat to weep, public weeping. The text humanizes the Egyptian governor — stripping away the official persona to reveal the wounded brother. Patristic and rabbinic readings have noted Joseph’s emotional control: he weeps in private but maintains the test in public. The interplay of love and necessary trial structures the entire reunion sequence — Joseph cannot yet reveal himself because the brothers have not yet completed their moral transformation.

↩ ◇ Note. Judah’s guarantee. Judah’s offer to personally guarantee Benjamin’s safety marks his moral transformation — the same Judah who proposed selling Joseph (37:26–27) now pledges himself for the youngest brother. The Hebrew root ʿarav (“to pledge, stand surety”) is the same root as Judah’s later great surety-speech at 44:18–34. The transformation becomes the chapter’s theological center: rebellion repented becomes responsibility offered. The pattern (a brother once willing to sell Joseph now pledging himself for Benjamin) is the moral arc Joseph has been waiting for.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s resignation. Jacob’s fatalistic “If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved” (closing the verse) parallels Esther 4:16 (“if I perish, I perish”). The language of resigned acceptance becomes a Hebrew-Bible motif of submission to providential plan even at apparent personal cost. Jacob’s invocation of El Shaddai (“God Almighty”) — the patriarchal divine name — is significant: at the moment of greatest fear, he reaches for the oldest covenant identification. The pairing of divine title with human resignation models prayer as both petition and surrender.

↩ ◇ Note. The brothers bow again. The second prostration — this time including Benjamin — fulfills the second part of Joseph’s sheaves dream more completely. The text seems to deliberately repeat the language of 42:6 (“bowed themselves down”), creating a doubled fulfillment that parallels the doubled dream itself. Joseph’s two dreams (sheaves, then sun-moon-stars) had different scopes; the dream-fulfillments unfold across multiple bowings. The narrative structure teaches that prophetic fulfillment can be staged across time — not all at once but in cumulative scenes.

↩ ◇ Note. Egyptian dietary separation. The text notes that Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews — an example of the rigid social-ethnic boundaries of ancient Egyptian culture. Egyptian sources confirm strong taboos around shared meals with foreigners, especially shepherds (the Hebrews’ primary occupation). The verse’s editorial interest is theological as much as ethnographic: Israel’s later separation laws (Exodus, Leviticus) will have analogues even within the Egyptian context. Acts 10–11 (Peter’s Cornelius vision) inverts the principle — the New Testament breaks down the table-fellowship boundary that Genesis 43:32 presupposes.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s divining cup. Joseph’s steward attributes divinatory practice to his master’s silver cup — hydromancy (water-divination by observing patterns in cup) was an Egyptian practice. The detail is layered: either Joseph genuinely uses divination (problematic given Mosaic prohibitions later), or the steward exaggerates for dramatic effect, or Joseph plays the role of an Egyptian official. Most commentators favor the third reading — the cup-divination is part of Joseph’s elaborate test-setup. The verse highlights how Joseph speaks within Egyptian categories while operating from covenant theology — bicultural performance, not actual divination.

↩ ◇ Note. Judah’s plea. Judah’s extended speech (44:18–34) is the longest single speech in Genesis — the most sustained piece of rhetoric the book contains. The speech rehearses the family history from a brother’s perspective, pleads for Benjamin’s release, and offers Judah himself as substitute. The literary craftsmanship is extraordinary: emotional appeal, narrative summary, legal argument, sacrificial offer all woven together. The speech transforms Judah from the brother who once profited from selling Joseph (37:26) to one offering himself in another’s place — the type of substitutionary love later read Christologically in Christian tradition.

↩ ◇ Note. God sent me. Joseph’s threefold statement that “God sent me” (45:5, 7, 8) gives the Joseph cycle its theological key. The brothers’ sale of Joseph is not undone or excused — but it is recontextualized within divine providence. The pattern of human evil employed for divine good becomes paradigmatic for biblical theology: the cross of Christ is the supreme instance (Acts 2:23, “delivered up by the determined plan and foreknowledge of God,” yet executed by lawless men). Joseph does not say his brothers did right; he says God overruled their wrong for life. The distinction is subtle but theologically crucial.

↩ ◇ Note. Preserving a remnant. Joseph’s reading of his Egyptian elevation as preservation of a “remnant” (sheʾerit, שְׁאֵרִית) introduces remnant theology into the patriarchal narrative. The same vocabulary structures the prophetic traditions (Isa 10:21–22 “a remnant will return”; Mic 4:7; Zech 8:6). The remnant concept becomes central to Pauline theology of Israel (Rom 9–11). Joseph’s exile, far from the line’s destruction, is its preservation — a paradoxical pattern that informs all biblical exile theology. The remnant is preserved by going down before going up.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. ʼerets (אֶרֶץ). the earth (at large, or partitively a land).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GOSHEN (1.) A district in Egypt where Jacob and his family settled, and in which they remained till the Exodus (Genesis 45:10; 46:28, 29, 31, etc.). It is called “the land of Goshen” (47:27), and also simply “Goshen” (46:28), and “the land of Rameses” (47:11; Exodus 12:37), for the towns Pithom and Rameses lay within its borders; also Zoan or Tanis (Psalm 78:12). It lay on the east of the Nile, and apparently not far from the royal residence. It was “the best of the land” (Genesis 47:6, 11), but is now a desert. It is first mentioned in Joseph’s message to his father. It has been identified with the modern Wady Tumilat, lying between the eastern part of the Delta and the west border of Palestine. It was a pastoral district, where some of the king’s cattle were kept (Genesis 47:6). The inhabitants were not exclusively Israelites (Exodus 3:22; 11:2; 12:35, 36). (2.) A district in Palestine (Joshua 10:41; 11:16). It was a part of the maritime plain of Judah, and lay between Gaza and Gibeon. (3.) A town in the mountains of Judah (Joshua 15:51).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MOSES drawn (or Egypt. mesu, “son;” hence Rameses, royal son). On the invitation of Pharaoh (Genesis 45:17-25), Jacob and his sons went down into Egypt. This immigration took place probably about 350 years before the birth of Moses. Some centuries before Joseph, Egypt had been conquered by a pastoral Semitic race from Asia, the Hyksos, who brought into cruel subjection the native Egyptians, who were an African race. Jacob and his retinue were accustomed to a shepherd’s life, and on their arrival in Egypt were received with favour by the king, who assigned them the “best of the land”, the land of Goshen, to dwell in. The Hyksos or “shepherd” king who thus showed favour to Joseph and his family was in all probability the Pharaoh Apopi (or Apopis). Thus favoured, the Israelites began to “multiply exceedingly” (Genesis 47:27), and extended to the west and south. At length the supremacy of the Hyksos came to an end. The descendants of Jacob were allowed to retain their possession of Goshen undisturbed, but after the death of Joseph their position was not so favourable. The Egyptians began to despise them, and the period of their “affliction” (Genesis 15:13) commenced. They were sorely oppressed. They continued, however, to increase in numbers, and “the land was filled with them” (Exodus 1:7). The native Egyptians regarded them with suspicion, so that they felt all the hardship of a struggle for existence. In process of time “a king [probably Seti I.] arose who knew not Joseph” (Exodus 1:8). (See PHARAOH.) The circumstances of the country were such that this king thought it necessary to weaken his Israelite subjects by oppressing them, and by degrees reducing their number. They were accordingly made public slaves, and were employed in connection with his numerous buildings, especially in the erection of store-cities, temples, and palaces. The children of Israel were made to serve with rigour. Their lives were made bitter with hard bondage, and “all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour” (Exodus 1:13, 14). But this cruel oppression had not the result expected of reducing their number. On the contrary, “the more the Egyptians afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew” (Exodus 1:12). The king next tried, through a compact secretly made with the guild of midwives, to bring about the destruction of all the Hebrew male children that might be born. But the king’s wish was not rigorously enforced; the male children were spared by the midwives, so that “the people multiplied” more than ever. Thus baffled, the king issued a public proclamation calling on the people to put to death all the Hebrew male children by casting them into the river (Exodus 1:22). But neither by this edict was the king’s purpose effected. One of the Hebrew households into which this cruel edict of the king brought great alarm was that of Amram, of the family of the Kohathites (Exodus 6:16-20), who with his wife Jochebed and two children, Miriam, a girl of perhaps fifteen years of age, and Aaron, a boy of three years, resided in or near Memphis, the capital city of that time. In this quiet home a male child was born (B.C. 1571). His mother concealed him in the house for three months from the knowledge of the civic authorities. But when the task of concealment became difficult, Jochebed contrived to bring her child under the notice of the daughter of the king by constructing for him an ark of bulrushes, which she laid among the flags which grew on the edge of the river at the spot where the princess was wont to come down and bathe. Her plan was successful. The king’s daughter “saw the child; and behold the child wept.” The princess (see PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER [1]) sent Miriam, who was standing by, to fetch a nurse. She went and brought the mother of the child, to whom the princess said, “Take this child away, and nurse it for me, and I will give thee thy wages.” Thus Jochebed’s child, whom the princess called “Moses”, i.e., “Saved from the water” (Exodus 2:10), was ultimately restored to her. As soon as the natural time for weaning the child had come, he was transferred from the humble abode of his father to the royal palace, where he was brought up as the adopted son of the princess, his mother probably accompanying him and caring still for him. He grew up amid all the grandeur and excitement of the Egyptian court, maintaining, however, probably a constant fellowship with his mother, which was of the highest importance as to his religious belief and his interest in his “brethren.” His education would doubtless be carefully attended to, and he would enjoy all the advantages of training both as to his body and his mind. He at length became “learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22). Egypt had then two chief seats of learning, or universities, at one of which, probably that of Heliopolis, his education was completed. Moses, being now about twenty years of age, spent over twenty more before he came into prominence in Bible history. These twenty years were probably spent in military service. There is a tradition recorded by Josephus that he took a lead in the war which was then waged between Egypt and Ethiopia, in which he gained renown as a skilful general, and became “mighty in deeds” (Acts 7:22). After the termination of the war in Ethiopia, Moses returned to the Egyptian court, where he might reasonably have expected to be loaded with honours and enriched with wealth. But “beneath the smooth current of his life hitherto, a life of alternate luxury at the court and comparative hardness in the camp and in the discharge of his military duties, there had lurked from childhood to youth, and from youth to manhood, a secret discontent, perhaps a secret ambition. Moses, amid all his Egyptian surroundings, had never forgotten, had never wished to forget, that he was a Hebrew.” He now resolved to make himself acquainted with the condition of his countrymen, and “went out unto his brethren, and looked upon their burdens” (Exodus 2:11). This tour of inspection revealed to him the cruel oppression and bondage under which they everywhere groaned, and could not fail to press on him the serious consideration of his duty regarding them. The time had arrived for his making common cause with them, that he might thereby help to break their yoke of bondage. He made his choice accordingly (Hebrews 11:25-27), assured that God would bless his resolution for the welfare of his people. He now left the palace of the king and took up his abode, probably in his father’s house, as one of the Hebrew people who had for forty years been suffering cruel wrong at the hands of the Egyptians. He could not remain indifferent to the state of things around him, and going out one day among the people, his indignation was roused against an Egyptian who was maltreating a Hebrew. He rashly lifted up his hand and slew the Egyptian, and hid his body in the sand. Next day he went out again and found two Hebrews striving together. He speedily found that the deed of the previous day was known. It reached the ears of Pharaoh (the “great Rameses,” Rameses II.), who “sought to slay Moses” (Exodus 2:15). Moved by fear, Moses fled from Egypt, and betook himself to the land of Midian, the southern part of the peninsula of Sinai, probably by much the same route as that by which, forty years afterwards, he led the Israelites to Sinai. He was providentially led to find a new home with the family of Reuel, where he remained for forty years (Acts 7:30), under training unconsciously for his great life’s work. Suddenly the angel of the Lord appeared to him in the burning bush (Exodus 3), and commissioned him to go down to Egypt and “bring forth the children of Israel” out of bondage. He was at first unwilling to go, but at length he was obedient to the heavenly vision, and left the land of Midian (4:18-26). On the way he was met by Aaron (q.v.) and the elders of Israel (27-31). He and Aaron had a hard task before them; but the Lord was with them (ch. 7-12), and the ransomed host went forth in triumph. (See EXODUS.) After an eventful journey to and fro in the wilderness, we see them at length encamped in the plains of Moab, ready to cross over the Jordan into the Promised Land. There Moses addressed the assembled elders (Deuteronomy 1:1-4; 5:1-26:19; 27:11-30:20), and gives the people his last counsels, and then rehearses the great song (Deuteronomy 32), clothing in fitting words the deep emotions of his heart at such a time, and in review of such a marvellous history as that in which he had acted so conspicious a part. Then, after blessing the tribes (33), he ascends to “the mountain of Nebo (q.v.), to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho” (34:1), and from thence he surveys the land. “Jehovah shewed him all the land of Gilead, unto Dan, and all Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim, and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah, unto the utmost sea, and the south, and the plain of the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees, unto Zoar” (Deuteronomy 34:2-3), the magnificient inheritance of the tribes of whom he had been so long the leader; and there he died, being one hundred and twenty years old, according to the word of the Lord, and was buried by the Lord “in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor” (34:6). The people mourned for him during thirty days. Thus died “Moses the man of God” (Deuteronomy 33:1; Joshua 14:6). He was distinguished for his meekness and patience and firmness, and “he endured as seeing him who is invisible.” “There arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and the wonders, which the Lord sent him to do in the land of Egypt to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land, and in all that mighty hand, and in all the great terror which Moses shewed in the sight of all Israel” (Deuteronomy 34:10-12). The name of Moses occurs frequently in the Psalms and Prophets as the chief of the prophets. In the New Testament he is referred to as the representative of the law and as a type of Christ (John 1:17; 2 Corinthians 3:13-18; Hebrews 3:5, 6). Moses is the only character in the Old Testament to whom Christ likens himself (John 5:46; comp. Deuteronomy 18:15, 18, 19; Acts 7:37). In Hebrews 3:1-19 this likeness to Moses is set forth in various particulars. In Jude 1:9 mention is made of a contention between Michael and the devil about the body of Moses. This dispute is supposed to have had reference to the concealment of the body of Moses so as to prevent idolatry.

↩ ◇ Note. Reversed sale. Joseph gives Benjamin three hundred shekels of silver — a startling counter to the twenty pieces of silver for which Joseph himself was sold (37:28). The detail dramatizes reversal: Joseph, sold for silver, now distributes silver. The five sets of clothing also echo the “coat of many colors” (37:3) that triggered the brothers’ resentment — Joseph now multiplies his clothing-gift fivefold, perhaps testing whether the gift-asymmetry that once produced rage now produces gratitude. The chapter’s restoration theology is enacted not just in words but in inverted economic exchanges.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s fainting. Jacob’s heart “grows numb” (Hebrew vayafag libbo) at the news that Joseph lives — too good to believe. The shocked-disbelief reaction parallels Luke 24:41 (the disciples disbelieving the resurrection “for joy”). The pattern teaches that great good news is harder to receive than bad news — the human heart, defended against further loss, struggles to receive resurrection. Jacob’s gradual transition from disbelief to acceptance (45:27, “the spirit of Jacob their father revived”) becomes a model for slow recognition of restoration.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: JACOB, PARENTS, WAGON.

↩ ◇ Note. Israel’s resolve. Jacob’s transformation in this verse is signaled by his name — “Israel said” (not Jacob). The grief-defined patriarch becomes the resolved patriarch: he will go to Egypt to see Joseph before dying. The single line completes Jacob’s narrative arc — the trickster transformed by loss is now the patriarch ready to descend into Egypt for the family’s preservation. The descent into Egypt sets up the entire Exodus narrative: the family’s preservation comes through the very land that will become their later bondage. The mixture of preservation and pre-figured suffering becomes the dialectic of biblical exile.

↩ ◇ Note. Visions of the night. Jacob receives the last patriarchal night-vision (cf. 28:12, the Bethel ladder; 31:11, return-from-Laban dream; 32:24, Jabbok wrestling). The Hebrew marʾot ha-laylah (“visions of the night”) is rare phrasing — appearing here, in Job 4:13 and 33:15, and in Daniel’s dream-visions (Dan 2:19, 7:2). The phrase typically marks especially significant theophanic communications. The double-call (“Jacob, Jacob”) imitates earlier patriarchal calls (Abraham at 22:11, Moses at Ex 3:4, Samuel at 1 Sam 3:10) — formal address that signals high-stakes covenantal speech.

↩ ◇ Note. The Exodus promise. God’s promise to Jacob — “I will surely bring you up again” — anticipates the entire Exodus narrative four centuries before it begins. The verb aʿaleh (“I will bring up”) becomes the standard verb for the Exodus event. The Israel-in-Egypt narrative is here framed not as exile but as preservation-with-promised-return. The verse anchors the eventual Exodus in patriarchal divine speech rather than emerging spontaneously at Moses’s call. The continuity of covenant promise across the long Egyptian sojourn is theologically central: God’s word at the descent already contains the ascent.

↩ ◇ Note. Genealogy framing the descent. The full genealogical list (46:8–27) frames the descent into Egypt with the named tribal patriarchs — preserving family identity at the moment of geographic transition. The same opening phrase (“These are the names of the children of Israel”) becomes the title of the next book (Exodus 1:1). The literary continuity directly links Genesis 46 to Exodus 1, treating the narrative as a single arc despite the book division. The genealogical inclusio frames Egypt as a chapter in family history, not a destination.

↩ ◇ Note. Seventy souls. The total of seventy descendants entering Egypt becomes a foundational number — Deut 10:22 reaffirms it; Acts 7:14 raises it to 75 (following the LXX). Seventy is symbolically resonant: the seventy nations of Genesis 10, the seventy elders of Exodus 24:9 and Numbers 11:16, the seventy years of Babylonian exile (Jer 25:11), the seventy disciples Jesus sends out (Luke 10:1). The number signals fullness or completeness — the entire family of Israel descends in a single, theologically significant unit. The discrepancy with 75 in LXX/Acts arises from inclusion of additional descendants of Joseph.

↩ ◇ Note. Shepherd abomination. The Egyptian disgust for shepherds reflects historical context. Egyptian sources (esp. from the Middle Kingdom) record contempt for nomadic herders, possibly intensified by the experience of the Hyksos — Asiatic shepherd-rulers who controlled Egypt c. 1650–1550 BCE. Joseph’s strategy of placing the family in Goshen (the Nile Delta) keeps them physically separated from Egyptian society — preserving distinct identity through geographic concentration. The same separation becomes the precondition for Israel’s later coherent slave-experience and group-Exodus rather than dispersed assimilation.

↩ ◇ Note. Goshen. Goshen, in the eastern Nile Delta, becomes the geographic stage for Israel’s entire Egyptian sojourn (Exodus 8:22, 9:26 specify it as the land where Israelites lived during the plagues). Modern archaeology associates Goshen with the area around Tell el-Dabʿa / Avaris — a region inhabited by Asiatic populations during the Second Intermediate Period. The narrative’s Goshen-grant fits well with the historical pattern of Asiatic settlement in Egypt’s eastern Delta. The specificity of the geographic detail anchors the patriarchal narrative in concrete archaeological geography.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s economic centralization. Joseph’s famine-administration progressively transfers all Egyptian wealth to Pharaoh: first money, then livestock (47:16–17), then land (47:20), finally the people themselves as servants (47:21). The narrative’s apparent endorsement of this system is striking — Joseph functions as economic centralizer and effectively reduces Egypt to royal property. Modern readings have found this troubling: the same patriarchal narrative that critiques Pharaoh’s later oppression of Israel here describes Joseph’s role in establishing absolute Egyptian royal economy. Some commentators (Brueggemann) read the chapter as morally ambivalent commentary on famine-driven state power.

↩ ◇ Note. Becoming Pharaoh’s servants. The Egyptians’ acceptance of slavery as gratitude for survival anticipates Israel’s later condition — “servants of Pharaoh” (ʿavadim le-Pharʿoh). The terminology becomes the standard Hebrew vocabulary for slavery (cf. Ex 5:15, Israel’s complaint as “your servants”). The narrative-layered irony is heavy: Joseph creates the institutional framework that his descendants will suffer under. The verse can be read as theologically quiet but morally pointed — accepting servitude for survival becomes the structural template that traps Israel for four centuries. The exodus event undoes what Joseph’s policies inaugurated.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s burial-oath. Jacob’s oath to Joseph — by the same hand-under-thigh formula Abraham used (24:2) — secures burial in the patriarchal tomb. The oath is theological as much as funerary: Jacob refuses to be buried in Egypt because Egypt is not the promised land. The body’s geography matters; identity persists in burial-place. The oath’s fulfillment (50:13, Joseph carries his father’s body to Machpelah) becomes the model for Joseph’s own analogous oath about his bones (50:25). The corpse-promises maintain land-orientation across generations — the bodies wait for the eventual return.

↩ ◇ Note. Recalling the Bethel theophany. Jacob recalls the Bethel/Luz theophany of 28:13–15 as he prepares to bless Joseph’s sons — anchoring his patriarchal blessing in the original divine promise. The pattern of patriarchal blessings citing original divine promises becomes paradigmatic: covenant transmission requires explicit memory of foundational theophanies. Jacob’s selection of El Shaddai as the divine name preserves the patriarchal divine epithet rather than using Yahweh — fitting the theological scheme of Exodus 6:3 (“I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as God Almighty; but by my name Yahweh I was not known to them”).

↩ ◇ Note. The crossed hands. Jacob’s deliberate crossing of his hands — putting his right (the hand of greater blessing) on the younger Ephraim — repeats the pattern that has structured the patriarchal narratives: younger over elder. Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph over the elder brothers, Perez over Zerah, now Ephraim over Manasseh. Jacob’s intentional inversion (48:14, “guiding his hands wittingly”) makes the pattern explicit — the inversion is not accidental but selected. Joseph’s protest (48:17–18) tries to correct what is intentional, leading to Jacob’s emphatic declaration that he knows. The pattern continues even into priestly blessing: God repeatedly chooses the unexpected.

↩ ◇ Note. Shepherd-God. Jacob’s blessing introduces shepherd-imagery for God (Hebrew haRoʿeh oti, “the one who has shepherded me”) — the first explicit shepherd-God title in Scripture. The image becomes Davidic (Ps 23:1, “Yahweh is my shepherd”) and reaches Christological climax (John 10:11, “I am the good shepherd”). Jacob’s life as wanderer-shepherd has formed his theological vocabulary: God as shepherd over a sheep-life. The triplet — God of fathers, God who shepherds, redeeming angel (48:15–16) — gives a fuller patriarchal name to deity than appears elsewhere in Genesis.

↩ ◇ Note. The redeeming angel. The “angel who has redeemed me from all harm” parallels but does not equate with the “God who has shepherded me” of the previous verse. The redeemer-angel may refer to the Jabbok wrestler (32:24), or be a distinct mediating figure. The Hebrew goʾel (“redeemer, kinsman-redeemer”) is a key Hebrew Bible category — invoked in Job 19:25 (“my Redeemer lives”), Ruth’s redeemer-figure, and ultimately in messianic theology. Jacob’s invocation of God-as-Redeemer is the first use of this vocabulary in Scripture, anchoring the redeemer-theology in patriarchal experience.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: BIRTHRIGHT, EPHRAIM, FIRSTBORN, INTERCESSION, MANASSEH, NAPHTALI, REUBEN, SIMEON, ZEBULUN.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: First Born, The, Parents.

↩ ◇ Note. The blessing formula. Jacob’s words become the standardized Jewish blessing for sons — fathers traditionally bless their boys on Friday night with this formula (“May God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh”). For daughters, the corresponding blessing invokes the four matriarchs. The verse thus crosses from narrative into liturgical practice — a Genesis blessing-text becoming centuries of Jewish home liturgy. The chosen typology is significant: not Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, but specifically Ephraim and Manasseh — sons born in exile yet remaining covenant-faithful. The model for Diaspora sons is sons who flourished outside the land while preserving covenant identity.

↩ ◇ Note. The last days. Jacob’s introduction — “what shall happen to you in the last days” (Hebrew be-acharit ha-yamim) — uses the formula that becomes prophetic and apocalyptic eschatology’s standard idiom (Isa 2:2, Mic 4:1, Hos 3:5; in the NT, Acts 2:17 “in the last days”). Genesis 49 is thus framed not as ordinary patriarchal blessing but as eschatological prophecy. The blessings on the twelve sons function as predictions about tribal destiny in covenant time. The prophetic dimension informs the chapter’s status as one of the oldest poetic strata in the Hebrew Bible — and one of the most theologically charged.

↩ ◇ Note. Reuben — unstable as water. Reuben’s blessing — “unstable as water, you shall not have the preeminence” — encodes the punishment for his sleeping with Bilhah (35:22). Reuben loses the firstborn rights to Joseph (1 Chr 5:1) — the youngest’s elevation that has structured Genesis ends with the formal-poetic confirmation. The phrase pachaz ka-mayim (“unstable as water”) has become proverbial. The Reuben tribe never produces a major leader, judge, or king in biblical history — the prophecy’s fulfillment is unspectacular but consistent. The verse demonstrates that Genesis poetry contains not just blessings but ominous predictions of historical limitations.

↩ ◇ Note. Simeon and Levi divided. The “curse” on Simeon and Levi for the Shechem violence (ch 34) takes the form of dispersion. Simeon’s tribal allotment in Joshua 19:1–9 lies entirely within Judah’s territory — by the time of the conquest, Simeon has been functionally absorbed. Levi’s “dispersion” takes a different form: as the priestly tribe, Levites have no contiguous territory but cities scattered throughout Israel (Numbers 35; Joshua 21). The same curse — “divided in Jacob, scattered in Israel” — is fulfilled in opposite ways: Simeon shrinks; Levi sanctified. The pattern teaches that judgment can transform into vocation.

↩ ◇ Note. The Mighty One of Jacob. The divine epithet Avir Yaʿakov (אֲבִיר יַעֲקֹב, “Mighty One of Jacob”) is one of the patriarchal divine names — appearing also at Isa 1:24, 49:26, 60:16; Ps 132:2, 132:5. The epithet preserves a primitive theological vocabulary in which deity is named by relationship to a particular ancestor. The Joseph-blessing here uses unusual divine-name density (Mighty One of Jacob, Shepherd, Stone of Israel, God of your father, El Shaddai) — five distinct divine titles in two verses. The poetic intensity reflects Joseph’s special status as the most-blessed son and as the line that, within Israel, will produce the northern kingdom of Israel.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob’s death. The detail of Jacob “gathering up his feet into the bed” captures the actual physical motion of death — drawing the legs up before the final breath. The vocabulary is concrete and intimate; biblical death-scenes typically use the formulaic “gathered to his people” (here also, at the verse’s close), but this verse adds the bodily detail. The dying patriarch’s final action is to compose himself for death — agency preserved into the final moment. The same detail recurs at 1 Kings 2:1 (David’s death-preparation). Jacob’s deliberate death scene contrasts with the violent unprepared deaths that have shaped his life.

↩ ◇ Note. The royal funeral procession. Joseph’s funeral procession for Jacob includes Egyptian officials and is conducted with seventy days of mourning (50:3) plus seven additional days at the threshing floor of Atad (50:10). The seventy-day mourning matches Egyptian royal funerary period for kings (Herodotus 2.86–88). The narrative quietly elevates Jacob to royal-funeral honors — the patriarch buried not as ordinary man but with ceremony befitting Egyptian state functionary. The detail signals Joseph’s full integration into Egyptian power structure while preserving Israelite identity through the Canaan-burial requirement.

↩ ◇ Note. The forgiveness petition. The brothers’ message to Joseph — invoking their dead father’s request for forgiveness — uses the strongest Hebrew vocabulary for sin (peshaʿ, “transgression”) and forgiveness (nasaʾ, “lift, bear, pardon”). The combination becomes paradigmatic for Hebrew Bible forgiveness theology: serious wrongdoing requires explicit acknowledgment and explicit forgiveness. Whether Jacob actually issued the request the brothers report is debated — many commentators read it as a face-saving fiction. Joseph’s response (50:19–21) extends forgiveness regardless of whether the petition was genuine. The pattern teaches that grace exceeds the worthiness of the petitioner.

↩ ◇ Note. God will visit you. Joseph’s death-bed prophecy — “God will surely visit you and bring you up out of this land” — echoes God’s promise to Jacob at 46:4 (“I will bring you up again”). The verb paqod yifqod (“surely visit”) is the same vocabulary used of Sarah’s miraculous conception (21:1, “Yahweh visited Sarah”) and becomes the standard Hebrew vocabulary for divine intervention. The phrase becomes Israel’s prophetic memory in Egypt — Exodus 3:16 has Moses say to the elders “Yahweh has surely visited you,” the language Joseph predicted. The verse establishes the Exodus framework before the Exodus events.

↩ ◇ Note. Joseph’s bones. Joseph extracts an oath from his brothers regarding his bones — paralleling Jacob’s burial oath. The oath is fulfilled at Exodus 13:19 (Moses takes Joseph’s bones at the Exodus) and Joshua 24:32 (Joshua buries them at Shechem). The bones become a mobile relic of covenant continuity — Israel literally carries Joseph through the wilderness and into the land. Hebrews 11:22 cites this verse as paradigmatic faith — Joseph’s confidence that the descent into Egypt was not the end of the story. The bones-vow theologizes the corpse: even in death, the patriarchs orient themselves toward the promised land.

↩ ◇ Note. Genesis ends in Egypt. The book closes with Joseph in a coffin in Egypt — a striking ending. The patriarchal narratives that began with God’s command to Abraham to “go from your country” (12:1) end with the entire family settled in foreign land, the chosen son embalmed Egyptian-style, awaiting future return. The coffin-in-Egypt ending creates structural tension that demands continuation: the promises remain unfulfilled in the land, the people are outside it. Exodus picks up directly from this hanging note. Genesis is thus structurally incomplete — it requires Exodus, and ultimately Joshua, to complete its arc. The book of beginnings ends in promised-but-not-yet.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JUDAH praise, the fourth son of Jacob by Leah. The name originated in Leah’s words of praise to the Lord on account of his birth: “Now will I praise [Hebrews odeh] Jehovah, and she called his name Yehudah” (Genesis 29:35). It was Judah that interposed in behalf of Joseph, so that his life was spared (Genesis 37:26, 27). He took a lead in the affairs of the family, and “prevailed above his brethren” (Genesis 43:3-10; 44:14, 16-34; 46:28; 1 Chronicles 5:2). Soon after the sale of Joseph to the Ishmaelites, Judah went to reside at Adullam, where he married a woman of Canaan. (See ONAN; TAMAR.) After the death of his wife Shuah, he returned to his father’s house, and there exercised much influence over the patriarch, taking a principal part in the events which led to the whole family at length going down into Egypt. We hear nothing more of him till he received his father’s blessing (Genesis 49:8-12).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CHESTNUT TREE (Hebrews ’armon; i.e., “naked”), mentioned in connection with Jacob’s artifice regarding the cattle (Genesis 30:37). It is one of the trees of which, because of its strength and beauty, the Assyrian empire is likened (Ezekiel 31:8; R.V., “plane trees”). It is probably the Oriental plane tree (Platanus orientalis) that is intended. It is a characteristic of this tree that it annually sheds its outer bark, becomes “naked.” The chestnut tree proper is not a native of Palestine.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HAZEL Hebrews luz, (Genesis 30:37), a nutbearing tree. The Hebrew word is rendered in the Vulgate by amygdalinus, “the almond-tree,” which is probably correct. That tree flourishes in Syria.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PLANE TREE Hebrews ‘armon (Genesis 30:37; Ezekiel 31:8), rendered “chesnut” in the Authorized Version, but correctly “plane tree” in the Revised Version and the LXX. This tree is frequently found in Palestine, both on the coast and in the north. It usually sheds its outer bark, and hence its Hebrew name, which means “naked.” (See CHESTNUT.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). POPLAR Hebrews libneh, “white”, (Genesis 30:37; Hos. 4:13), in all probability the storax tree (Styrax officinalis) or white poplar, distinguished by its white blossoms and pale leaves. It is common in the Anti-Libanus. Other species of the poplar are found in Palestine, such as the white poplar (P. alba) of our own country, the black poplar (P. nigra), and the aspen (P. tremula). (See WILLOW.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HALT lame on the feet (Genesis 32:31; Psalm 38:17). To “halt between two opinions” (1 Kings 18:21) is supposed by some to be an expression used in “allusion to birds, which hop from spray to spray, forwards and backwards.” The LXX. render the expression “How long go ye lame on both knees?” The Hebrew verb rendered “halt” is used of the irregular dance (“leaped upon”) around the altar (ver. 26). It indicates a lame, uncertain gait, going now in one direction, now in another, in the frenzy of wild leaping.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HARLOT (1.) Hebrews zonah (Genesis 34:31; 38:15). In verses 21, 22 the Hebrew word used in kedeshah, i.e., a woman consecrated or devoted to prostitution in connection with the abominable worship of Asherah or Astarte, the Syrian Venus. This word is also used in Deuteronomy 23:17; Hos. 4:14. Thus Tamar sat by the wayside as a consecrated kedeshah. It has been attempted to show that Rahab, usually called a “harlot” (Joshua 2:1; 6:17; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25), was only an innkeeper. This interpretation, however, cannot be maintained. Jephthah’s mother is called a “strange woman” (Judges 11:2). This, however, merely denotes that she was of foreign extraction. In the time of Solomon harlots appeared openly in the streets, and he solemnly warns against association with them (Proverbs 7:12; 9:14. See also Jeremiah 3:2; Ezekiel 16:24, 25, 31). The Revised Version, following the LXX., has “and the harlots washed,” etc., instead of the rendering of the Authorized Version, “now they washed,” of 1 Kings 22:38. To commit fornication is metaphorically used for to practice idolatry (Jeremiah 3:1; Ezekiel 16:15; Hos. throughout); hence Jerusalem is spoken of as a harlot (Isaiah 1:21). (2.) Hebrews nokriyah, the “strange woman” (1 Kings 11:1; Proverbs 5:20; 7:5; 23:27). Those so designated were Canaanites and other Gentiles (Joshua 23:13). To the same class belonged the “foolish”, i.e., the sinful, “woman.” In the New Testament the Greek pornai, plural, “harlots,” occurs in Matthew 21:31,32, where they are classed with publicans; Luke 15:30; 1 Corinthians 6:15,16; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25. It is used symbolically in Revelation 17:1, 5, 15, 16; 19:2.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Isaac gave up the ghost, and died... and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him'. Ephrem notes the symmetric structure with Abraham's burial (25:9 — both half-brothers reconciled at the patriarchal burial). The pattern persists: covenant-divisions soften at death; the family-of-the-promise gathers at the threshold. Tewahedo funerary theology preserves this as the canonical pattern for inter-family reconciliation: estranged kin reconcile at the threshold of ancestral burial.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CHAMBERLAIN a confidential servant of the king (Genesis 37:36; 39:1). In Romans 16:23 mention is made of “Erastus the chamberlain.” Here the word denotes the treasurer of the city, or the quaestor, as the Romans styled him. He is almost the only convert from the higher ranks of whom mention is made (comp. Acts 17:34). Blastus, Herod’s “chamberlain” (Acts 12:20), was his personal attendant or valet-de-chambre. The Hebrew word saris, thus translated in Esther 1:10, 15; 2:3, 14, 21, etc., properly means an eunuch (as in the marg.), as it is rendered in Isaiah 39:7; 56:3.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GUARD (1.) Hebrews tabbah (properly a “cook,” and in a secondary sense “executioner,” because this office fell to the lot of the cook in Eastern countries), the bodyguard of the kings of Egypt (Genesis 37:36) and Babylon (2 Kings 25:8; Jeremiah 40:1; Daniel 2:14). (2.) Hebrews rats, properly a “courier,” one whose office was to run before the king’s chariot (2 Samuel 15:1; 1 Kings 1:5). The couriers were also military guards (1 Samuel 22:17; 2 Kings 10:25). They were probably the same who under David were called Pelethites (1 Kings 14:27; 2 Samuel 15:1). (3.) Hebrews mishmereth, one who watches (Nehemiah 4:22), or a watch-station (7:3; 12:9; Job 7:12). In the New Testament (Mark 6:27) the Authorized Version renders the Greek spekulator by “executioner,” earlier English versions by “hangman,” the Revised Version by “soldier of his guard.” The word properly means a “pikeman” or “halberdier,” of whom the bodyguard of kings and princes was composed. In Matthew 27:65, 66; 28:11, the Authorized Version renders the Greek kustodia by “watch,” and the Revised Version by “guard,” the Roman guard, which consisted of four soldiers, who were relieved every three hours (Acts 12:4). The “captain of the guard” mentioned Acts 28:16 was the commander of the Praetorian troops, whose duty it was to receive and take charge of all prisoners from the provinces.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EPHRAIM double fruitfulness (“for God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction”). The second son of Joseph, born in Egypt (Genesis 41:52; 46:20). The first incident recorded regarding him is his being placed, along with his brother Manasseh, before their grandfather, Jacob, that he might bless them (48:10; comp. 27:1). The intention of Joseph was that the right hand of the aged patriarch should be placed on the head of the elder of the two; but Jacob set Ephraim the younger before his brother, “guiding his hands wittingly.” Before Joseph’s death, Ephraim’s family had reached the third generation (Genesis 50:23).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EPHRAIM , THE TRIBE OF took precedence over that of Manasseh by virtue of Jacob’s blessing (Genesis 41:52; 48:1). The descendants of Joseph formed two of the tribes of Israel, whereas each of the other sons of Jacob was the founder of only one tribe. Thus there were in reality thirteen tribes; but the number twelve was preserved by excluding that of Levi when Ephraim and Manasseh are mentioned separately (Numbers 1:32-34; Joshua 17:14, 17; 1 Chronicles 7:20). Territory of. At the time of the first census in the wilderness this tribe numbered 40,500 (Numbers 1:32, 33); forty years later, when about to take possession of the Promised Land, it numbered only 32,500. During the march (see CAMP) Ephraim’s place was on the west side of the tabernacle (Numbers 2:18-24). When the spies were sent out to spy the land, “Oshea the son of Nun” of this tribe signalized himself. The boundaries of the portion of the land assigned to Ephraim are given in Joshua 16:1-10. It included most of what was afterwards called Samaria as distinguished from Judea and Galilee. It thus lay in the centre of all traffic, from north to south, and from Jordan to the sea, and was about 55 miles long and 30 broad. The tabernacle and the ark were deposited within its limits at Shiloh, where it remained for four hundred years. During the time of the judges and the first stage of the monarchy this tribe manifested a domineering and haughty and discontented spirit. “For more than five hundred years, a period equal to that which elapsed between the Norman Conquest and the War of the Roses, Ephraim, with its two dependent tribes of Manasseh and Benjamin, exercised undisputed pre-eminence. Joshua the first conqueror, Gideon the greatest of the judges, and Saul the first king, belonged to one or other of the three tribes. It was not till the close of the first period of Jewish history that God ‘refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim, but chose the tribe of Judah, the Mount Zion which he loved’ (Psalm 78:67, 68). When the ark was removed from Shiloh to Zion the power of Ephraim was humbled.” Among the causes which operated to bring about the disruption of Israel was Ephraim’s jealousy of the growing power of Judah. From the settlement of Canaan till the time of David and Solomon, Ephraim had held the place of honour among the tribes. It occupied the central and fairest portions of the land, and had Shiloh and Shechem within its borders. But now when Jerusalem became the capital of the kingdom, and the centre of power and worship for the whole nation of Israel, Ephraim declined in influence. The discontent came to a crisis by Rehoboam’s refusal to grant certain redresses that were demanded (1 Kings 12).

'Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do' (Pharaoh's command to the famine-stricken people). Ephrem reads this verbatim as the Marian-Cana-prefiguration: 'whatsoever he saith unto you, do it' (Jn 2:5 — Mary's words to the servants at Cana). Tewahedo Marian theology preserves this typological pair: Joseph's authoritative mediation in famine prefigures Mary's authoritative mediation at Cana; both point to Christ as ultimate-provider.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HADES that which is out of sight, a Greek word used to denote the state or place of the dead. All the dead alike go into this place. To be buried, to go down to the grave, to descend into hades, are equivalent expressions. In the LXX. this word is the usual rendering of the Hebrew sheol, the common receptacle of the departed (Genesis 42:38; Psalm 139:8; Hos. 13:14; Isaiah 14:9). This term is of comparatively rare occurrence in the Greek New Testament. Our Lord speaks of Capernaum as being “brought down to hell” (hades), i.e., simply to the lowest debasement, (Matthew 11:23). It is contemplated as a kind of kingdom which could never overturn the foundation of Christ’s kingdom (16:18), i.e., Christ’s church can never die. In Luke 16:23 it is most distinctly associated with the doom and misery of the lost. In Acts 2:27-31 Peter quotes the LXX. version of Psalm 16:8-11, plainly for the purpose of proving our Lord’s resurrection from the dead. David was left in the place of the dead, and his body saw corruption. Not so with Christ. According to ancient prophecy (Psalm 30:3) he was recalled to life.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)
